subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF GRANT FOR HEALTH SCIENCES CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce that the government proposes the expenditure of $4 million to assist in the design and construction of a health sciences centre at the University of British Columbia. This is a special pilot project, outside and apart from our health grants program, and will be provided for in my departmental estimates later this year.
The development of such a centre at the University of British Columbia has been under study for a number of years. It will establish a new concept in the training of the health professions and has been strongly endorsed by medical health educators.
The amount authorized by the government, which is conditional upon at least an equal amount being provided by the provincial government, will be made available in instalments as planning and construction progress. It is expected that up to two years' planning will be required before construction can begin.

Health Sciences Centre
The new centre will be primarily a teaching institution, but will also provide a 410 bed hospital with extensive research facilities. It is also to be used for the referral of patients needing the special services and facilities contained in such a unit.
In authorizing this provisional grant the government is aware of the importance of the teaching pattern developed at this university in providing common instruction facilities for all health provisions, doctors, dentists, pharmacists, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, social workers and psychologists.
This team approach to teaching is considered a major advance in medical education and should have an important impact on the quality of health care, particularly in the face of future developments regarding the provision of health services. The improvement in the method of teaching should also encourage the entry of more young people into the health professions.
This pioneer project may well establish an important pattern for future development and the government, for this reason, considers that a special grant for this important purpose is fully warranted.

The management of the Canadian National Railways advise that the company's decision on its trademark is contained in a press release issued on December 15, 1960, and from which the following extracts have been taken as explanatory information in reply to the question:
"The trademark, developed and tested during the past year, began appearing on the sides of box cars at the same time that C.N. employees were introduced to the symbol in

the December-January issue of the railways' employee magazine "Keeping Track".
Designed by Toronto's Allan Fleming, the trademark is a continuous line forming the letters "C.N." to express movement-the movement of men, messages and materials.
The traditional "R" has been eliminated because the trademark must service C.N.'s multi-type business-hotels, communications, express, freight and passenger services. As well, "C.N." is bilingual; "C.N.R." is not.
The new trademark is the first step in a comprehensive redesign program launched by the C.N. in the summer of 1959. The decision to embark on the program followed a survey on public attitudes conducted across Canada. The survey showed that in spite of centralized traffic control, dieselization, modern electronic hump yards, new microwave facilities and other modern programs being carried out by the railway, the public still regarded Canadian National and railways generally as old-fashioned and slow about trying to find new ways of improving their operations and service to the public.
The program is built around the new C.N. symbol, but a great deal of attention is being given to the backgrounds against which the trademark will be applied: color schemes for trains, trucks, uniforms, signs, telegraph blanks, stations, letterheads, and all the many items involved in C.N.'s businesses."

TEST EXAMINATION OF GOVERNMENT ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
1.	What criteria determine the test basis for the examination of accounts by the Auditor General?
2.	Referring to the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1963, at p. 3, what in detail and with full particulars were the "too many instances where staff shortages result in the audit office being unable to carry out its test examinations with sufficient frequency or in sufficient depth to achieve even the minimum standard required by modem accepted auditing practice"?
3.	What is "modem accepted auditing practice" referred to in this statement and in what particulars has it been departed from?
4.	What is the minimum standard of such practice and in what particulars has it not been achieved in any department specifying such department?
5.	In what departments or branches of departments were the test examinations carried out with insufficient depth?
6.	In respect of each of these departments or branches of departments (a) what in particular was the lack of depth (b) what would have been a sufficient depth?
7.	In what departments or branches of departments were the test examinations carried out with insufficient frequency?
8.	In respect of these (a) what was the frequency (b) what would have been sufficient frequency?
Answer: 1. When the Auditor General states that his examinations of the accounts have included such tests as he considered necessary in the circumstances, he means that he has examined portions of the transactions, supporting documents and records to the extent that he deems necessary in order to form an independent opinion as to the correctness of the accounts.
The auditing procedure of testing or sampling represents an inspection of a sample of items selected from the transactions of the period under review with the object of judging the degree of reliability and quality of the whole on the basis of the sample. One of the most important factors to be taken into consideration in determining the extent of testing required is the effectiveness of the existing system of internal control which is reviewed by the Auditor General. Other factors include the reliability of the accounting records, the risk of the existence of signficant errors and the relative importance of the transactions to be tested. The extent of testing in any examination is a matter of the auditor's judgment which is recognized by the employment of the words "The Auditor

Questions
General shall examine in such manner as he may deem necessary" in the Financial Administration Act.
2.	The statement quoted from page 3 of the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1963 to the House of Commons was also made by him in his report to the House of Commons for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1962.
It would not be in the public interest were the Auditor General to make known in detail and with full particulars those instances where his test examinations have not been carried out with sufficient frequency or in sufficient depth to achieve even the minimum standard required by modern accepted auditing practice.
3.	Modern accepted auditing practice may be defined in general as the examination of accounting documents and supporting evidence for the purpose of reaching an informed opinion concerning their propriety. As in the case under (2) above, it would not be in the public interest to reveal the extent to which this has been departed from.
4.	5, 6, 7 and 8. As mentioned in the answers to (2) and (3) above, it is not in the public interest to disclose the extent to which the audit office has been unable to carry out its test examinations with sufficient frequency or in sufficient depth to achieve even the minimum standard required by modern accepted auditing practice.

subtopic: VALUE OF SAINT JOHN RIVER
VALUE OF SAINT JOHN RIVER
speechtext:
Carleton):
Has the Atlantic development board any information concerning the present and potential value of the Saint John river, especially that portion affected by the Mactaquac project, in its natural state?

subtopic: VALUE OF SAINT JOHN RIVER
speechtext:
I am advised by the Atlantic development board as follows:
It would be extremely difficult to assign meaningful quantitative values to the various features and aspects of the Saint John river, present and potential.
The Saint John river is, of course, well known for its salmon fishery, both commercial and sport. There are, however, widely differing estimates of the real value to the economy of the salmon sport fishery.
The river and valley have great natural beauty. To date, commercial development for recreation and tourism has not occurred on any large scale. The control of pollution, a serious problem in the river at present, is essential to the full development of the recreational and tourist value of the river. There is reason to believe the potential of the river for tourism and recreation will also be greatly enhanced by the creation of a 50 mile lake above the dam consequent upon the Mactaquac power development, particularly if steps are taken to deal with pollution.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, June 29, consideration in committee of Bill C-90, to amend the National Defence Act-Mr. Hellyer -Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Duties of chief of the defence staff.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order. The house again in committee of the whole on Bill No. C-90, to amend the National Defence Act. Shall clause 1 carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill before the committee provides for only one thing of importance; that is the abolition of the chiefs of staff of the navy, the army and the air force, and the substitution for them of one chief of defence staff. However, the debate on second reading, and particularly the proceedings and the evidence which we secured in the defence committee, show that a great deal more is involved than this; or rather, that a great deal more will flow from it.
What is actually proposed and what will result from the passage of this bill is a complete reorganization of the military side of defence headquarters. The present organization of defence headquarters is based on the existence of the three services, the navy, army and air force, each with its own head and its own definite line of command and communication running down to individual units. What is proposed is the disappearance of these three chiefs of staff and their headquarters staffs, and a substitution for them of a single defence staff which will take over all the functions previously performed by these three separate staffs. However, Mr. Chairman, the three services will remain.

National Defence Act
This is provided for in the National Defence Act, and until it is changed we will still have the navy, army and air force.
One thing which was not made clear on second reading or in the evidence we secured in the defence committee was how the chain of command will operate. In particular, we received no evidence whatever as to whether the new system will not make for a great deal more confusion and will not be more cumbersome and less effective than the system we have at the present time. In my opinion this was one of the deficiencies in the evidence presented to the defence committee. Really all we had there was the unsupported word of the Minister of National Defence that in his opinion the new system would work better than the old. On the other hand we had evidence from people who had previously held important military positions that the reverse would be the situation.
One thing in particular I should like to draw to the attention of the committee is that under the new system it appears there will be at least four or perhaps five chains of command from the top down to the individual units, which in the final analysis will have to do any fighting or carry out other operations that may be required of them. I think this is clear from the chart provided to us in the committee showing the proposed new organization, in which under a chief of defence staff you have four main branches. As the minister indicated, this is an organization designed to operate on a functional basis rather than the service basis we have had in the past.
What we will have under this new system is a chief of operational readiness who will be responsible particularly for operational matters, for what used to be referred to generally as the "G" side or general staff side of any military organization. We have next a chief of personnel who will be responsible for recruiting, manning, personnel administration and services generally. Third, we have a chief of logistics and engineering, which function is again split into logistics generally on the one hand and engineering and development on the other. Under this would come, of course, transport, accommodation, the supply of food and all that sort of thing. Finally there is a comptroller general who is in charge of program management, establishment, organization generally and budgeting.
As I say, it would appear from this that as far as each individual unit or formation is concerned there will in effect be four bosses 
instead of one. You really have four distinct functions which are commanded by four separate people. So far as I can see you are going to have four channels of command and communication down to the people who in effect have to carry out the operation or do anything. Therefore I am doubtful, as I think a lot of other people are, whether this form of organization is not going to be more cumbersome, more difficult to operate and less effective and efficient than the one we have at the present time.
The basic purpose of the changes proposed is to secure unification of command and, from the minister's statements, the eventual unification of all the services. I have no quarrel with the idea of providing for unification of command. In fact, as I have said on other occasions, I think this is necessary and desirable. However, the method to be followed in order to secure this objective is a very different matter.
The United Kingdom, for example, has reorganized in order to secure unification of command, and various other countries have done the same thing; but they have done so on a basis completely different from the one proposed. I mention this merely to show that unification of command can be secured in other ways. The particular plan which has been put before us and which it is proposed to put into operation is by no means the only plan which could be followed in order to secure unification of command, and in the minds of a large number of people it is a considerably inferior plan and one not likely to work as effectively as, for example, the one that has been adopted in the United Kingdom.
In connection with the discussions we had in the defence committee in regard to this whole matter, the minister made out that one of the great virtues of his proposal was the cutting down of the channels of communication from the services to himself from six to three, in effect reducing his direct military advisers from four men to one man, from the present three chiefs of staff of the services plus the chairman of the chiefs of staff to a single chief of defence staff.
I submit this is a weakness rather than a strength. I think there is no question but that experience in this and in all other countries has shown that separate, independent military advice to the minister responsible for the defence activities of the country is an advantage rather than otherwise. For the minister in effect to make himself dependant on one source of military advice only handicaps

his ability, I think, to get at the real situation; to get independent and frequently differing opinions as to the course of action which should be followed. Thus I believe that under this new system the minister will be in a much poorer position to assess what should be done and what course to follow than would be the case under the sort of system we have had, where he has had the benefit of advice from the head of each of the separate services on how a particular problem is going to affect them, whether the solution proposed is practicable and so on.
This really comes down to what is frequently referred to as the supremo concept, having one supreme commander. This has been tried in the past. In fact this system was in effect in Great Britain up to 1904, when the Esher commission reported that the inefficiency and many of the semi-military disasters and difficulties that the British had experienced over almost 100 years following Waterloo up to that time, the difficulties they had had in the Indian mutiny, in the Crimean war, in Egypt and in the South African war, had arisen to a large extent because of the inability of one supreme commander to effectively control the military organization and give the proper type of advice to the minister responsible.
You had the same situation in Germany, where the chief of the general staff was the supreme military commander. This situation prevailed in Germany, of course, before 1914 and again under Hitler. In that case you had really a separate power and authority within the German state, and I believe most historians will agree this situation was responsible to a large extent for the catastrophe of the first world war.
Now, on the basis of history-and it is only on the basis of what has happened in the past that we can assess a proposal of this kind-I submit that the proposal to revert in Canada to the concept of one supreme commander is not a reasonable one or a good one. It is not likely to work out or to give us as efficient or effective defence forces as a modification or a reorganization of the present set-up in order to give the advantages of unification of command.
There has been a lot of criticism of this proposal, particularly as to what the effect will be if you take away the three chiefs of staff. Air Marshal Curtis, who was one of the witnesses before the defence committee, a former chief of the air staff, had this to say as recorded at page 164 of the committee report of June 9:
National Defence Act
I feel that to do away with the chiefs of staff Is a terrible thing to do to the services. I do not care what you do, you are not going to have one service immediately. You may get it in 20 years but, in the meantime, our services are going to go down hill both in respect of morale and spirit.
I feel the three different services are like ships without a rudder; they are tossing around on the sea without a chief or a leader to lead them. That is what the C.A.S. is, the same as the C.G.S. and the C.N.S. And, you cannot substitute a chairman who is removed two or three times and who is bound to be from one of the other services. He cannot possibly have the same intimate knowledge of every service that the chiefs have.
I do not believe there is any question about it; that is the general idea that is held by most senior officers who have occupied the position of chief of staff at one time or another in the past. I have heard this same opinion expressed by an other former chief of air staff and by some former high ranking army and naval officers. I do not believe there is any question about it, that to place the amount of work which is required in the hands of one man by having a single defence chief on whom all of the responsibility for organization and operation of the military forces falls, is to impose too heavy a burden. It is not possible for one man, no matter who he is, to carry out that responsibility successfully. In my experience certainly the chiefs of the navy, army and air force were always fully occupied, as was the chairman of the chiefs of staff. Now it is proposed that the work formerly done by these four men will be done by one man. I doubt very much whether it can be done as well or as effectively.
If I may turn from that for a moment, Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps the greatest weakness in the proposal is that the minister has no idea as to what will happen below defence headquarters. The only thing about which we heard in the defence committee was what was going to happen in the reorganization of defence headquarters. When questions were asked as to what was going to happen below defence headquarters, how this so-called unification or integration was going to work out in the field generally, the minister's only answer was "We do not know yet; this will all fall into place. This will develop after we have reorganized the staff at defence headquarters. Then that staff will go ahead and get the rest of the services integrated", or unified or something else along that line.
It seems to me that this is an extremely naive approach. It is starting to do something, starting to change a system completely, without any real idea where you are heading or

National Defence Act how you are going to get there. I would say the minister is like a man who is starting out on an unknown sea without a compass, without knowing really where he is going to arrive when he crosses the particular body of water immediately before him.
There has been a great deal of talk about the integration of the services. However, we have had no definition of what the minister means by that term. One time he talks about unification, another time he talks about integration; and so far as the members of the committee are concerned I think some of the questions that were asked indicated the minister was not able to supply a clear explanation of what he means by these terms. He has no clear concept in mind as to what integration is going to mean to the defence forces of this country below national headquarters itself.
This, of course, makes for a great deal of uncertainty and confusion on the part of the people in the defence forces. In the meantime the minister has said that 500 air crew are being discharged or have been given their notice. Statements have been made that there will be a reduction of some 10,000 personnel in the forces, and naturally this has caused uncertainty and worry on the part of the people in the defence forces. At the same time you find that bases are being closed down and ships are being decommissioned, so naturally under these circumstances you are going to have a considerable reduction in morale.
Unfortunately this is exactly what is happening in our defence forces. I think generally the morale of our defence forces was as high as any in the world, but the uncertainty that exists as to the future of the personnel, as to whether they are going to get the axe some time in the future, what their function is going to be, whether their units are going to disappear-all these things have had an extremely serious effect on morale.
This was mentioned by more than one witness, but Air Marshal Curtis mentioned the experience he had in talking to both senior and junior serving and retired officers of the services. At page 180 of the evidence he is reported as saying:
-I would think that a lot of our technical officers can go outside and earn twice as much money as they are getting in the service. I would not be surprised to see them start to go and take jobs which offer pay better than they can receive in the service.
Then I asked him this question:


I am very much afraid not only about technical people particularly but also about the actual fighting units and those in command positions and so on who are sufficiently able that they can get jobs quite readily in civilian life and they will be doing this in large numbers unless the present situation is cleared up.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is my feeling, yes.
I do not believe there is any doubt but that those who are acquainted with people who have served, and know personnel in the services, have had exactly the same experience as Air Marshal Curtis has had and as I have had. A considerable number of the people with whom I have talked in the services are very worried about the future of the services and about the future of defence in this country, as well as their own future. As a result of this, increasing numbers of them are looking about for outside jobs. We are in very grave danger of losing a considerable number of our best general service command officers and technical officers unless this uncertainty is brought to an end, and unless people can know definitely what the future is likely to hold for them.
The chief difficulty here is that the minister does not really understand the importance of morale, that you can quite easily destroy it and that it is extremely hard to rebuild. The course he has been following so far is one designed to break down morale, to destroy the spirit of the forces, and we are likely to get into a serious situation from that point of view, as I have indicated, unless something definite is done to reassure the men.
The chief difficulty along this line, as I have indicated, is that the minister seems to have no clear idea of what he means by integration of services or how this will take place. He was been unable to say what will happen so far as the services are concerned. On second reading I pointed out the distinction which must be made between the administrative and fighting units. I pointed out that the integration of administrative functions can take place and should take place, but integration or unification of fighting units will not work. It will destroy fighting effectiveness. You must continue to have a ship as a fighting unit, an air squadron as a fighting unit, an infantry battalion as a fighting unit, and so forth.
In that connection I gave two or three examples, one of which was that it would be impossible to send the commander of an artillery battery to command a destroyer escort. Anybody who has any knowledge of military matters knows that is the situation, but the reply the minister made on that oc-

casion has caused a great deal of dismay to a very large number of people in the services. This is what he said, as recorded at page 3188 of Hansard for May 12:
The hon. member said an artillery officer could not command a destroyer. That may be so, but I suspect that an artillery officer might find himself quite at home with a naval gun after a brief familiarization period. Certainly many of the basic skills involved are the same.
To anybody with any experience this was a very dismaying statement. The minister did not know what he was talking about. This is not a workable concept. It is one of the things which has added to the uncertainty, and to the idea in the minds of a lot of serving officers and other personnel that the minister does not know where he is heading or what he is doing. He went on to say:
I think there should be no doubt left in anyone's mind as to what is intended. This unification of the command of the three armed forces is, as stated in the white paper, intended to be the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.
The only meaning you can take out of that is that all the present units, organizations and what not are going to disappear. But in giving evidence before the committee, at one point the minister said "Well, of course, the present naval units and army units and air force units will continue." As I have pointed out previously, it is essential that they should continue. You cannot have fighting forces unless you have units of this kind, but the minister's statements are contradictory and confusing to people. As a result neither the general public nor the people in the armed forces who are most affected, and whose general efficiency is at stake, know what the minister means or where he is headed. I hope this situation will be cleared up rapidly, and that a definite statement will be made as to what is going to happen below defence headquarters level.
If the minister still has any idea that by integration all the fighting units are going to be rolled into one shapeless mass, then the sooner he comes to realize that that is impractical and would destroy the fighting effectiveness of our forces the better off he, the government, the country and the defence forces will be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in taking part in this debate on Bill No. C-90, I should like to point out briefly that the subject of the bill in itself covers a somewhat narrow field of action since it limits the debate, I think, to the appointment of a chief of defence staff, who would replace the com-
National Dejence Act
mittee which was presided over by the chief of staff of the armed forces.
This bill comes within the over-all project of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), providing for the unification of the armed forces and a rather substantial reduction in the number of servicemen. I believe that the step we are taking today is a step in the right direction.
If this debate is to be rather limited in time, it is merely because the question has been discussed at length by the defence committee. In my opinion, we had at that stage the opportunity of getting the information we sought, even if the replies were not always quite satisfactory and in line with the ideas one might have on the subject.
I feel that the reduction of our military forces is a good way of saving Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars. However, I should like to repeat here what I said in committee. It seems to me that the chief of defence staff, who will make the decisions, under the minister, will still have to be surrounded by advisers because he will be unable to make all the decisions by himself. He will have to take into account the recommendations made by the experts around him.
When you consider the military development in this country and see the mistakes made time and again in the procurement of defence material, the efficiency of those people is doubtful, if they continue to have the same advisers as before, the same men who, for instance, favoured the development of the Arrow aircraft, or the construction of the Bobcat military vehicles, or those who encouraged the government to acquire submarines in England.
When, in the past, those individuals made some mistakes which, today, are deplored and criticized from all sides, I wonder what we can expect if, in the years to come, we continue to employ those supposed experts in matters of defence, who nevertheless, encouraged the government to buy equipment which proved obsolete, after being only a short time in use, involving considerable expenditure of the Canadian taxpayers' money.
Mr. Chairman, I think that this is both a most sensitive and delicate point, because in the rapid evolution which is taking place at this time in the technological field, it is certainly difficult to establish what result machinery which it is proposed to buy at this time may give in the years to come, and how long it may remain efficient, before being replaced. Indeed, if, today, we buy some equipment which will eventually be

National Defence Act
replaced tomorrow because it has become obsolete, I wonder again if we should not, at that time, simply avoid expenses as considerable as in the past, because Canada cannot afford to spend such considerable amounts as our neighbours to the south for buying equipment which, to all ends and purposes, will become obsolete the next day.
The minister will probably have to give special consideration to the recommendations he will receive from the military experts, because the general public is always asking itself certain questions. Indeed, the question is often asked: why did they buy that, if it will not be any good tomorrow? That is when it is rather hard to explain such expenditures to the taxpayers and to answer their questions, when we realize what is going on almost everywhere and we see how money is spent in the field of military defence.
Many taxpayers tell us about things happening in military camps, with special emphasis on the waste of public funds, the misuse of equipment and of everything available to the soldiers. Naturally, I do not intend to go into details, because I realize people are inclined to exaggerate some of the irregularities that may have been committed.
Moreover, I understand that, in the administration of such an important department, mistakes and squandering are unavoidable, but I think that the department should have a special committee, made up of people outside the Department of National Defence and whose members would not be responsible even to the chief of staff, who could go from one military camp to another to check on the spot what is going on and prevent abuses, if any, and see whether it would not be possible to save the equipment and the time of the men now in the armed forces.
Mr. Chairman, there is another point which I would like to discuss briefly and I think that I could do so now. I refer to our military colleges and our young people who are contemplating a career in the armed forces.
Since the total establishment will be reduced, the minister will have to rely on markedly improved equipment and on efficient men. I am not suggesting that our present military leaders have no knowledge or efficiency. Far from it. I feel that our military personnel is intelligent, but I think personally that our military colleges should be given more importance so as to train men with a broader outlook than that of soldiers who rose from the ranks and were promoted after many years of service or because of experience acquired in the armed forces. I know

that experience is an excellent thing, that it is a supplement, but I feel that basic education is most important and will greatly help our future military men to take charge of rather large units to which they will have to give the training they received themselves.
In short, one might say that the army should insist on quality rather than on quantity and try to improve its efficiency.
In this connection, I cannot help thinking of our military colleges, and I hope that it will be possible to extend the curriculum in order to encourage our young people to stay there after they have received their training. As a matter of fact, we see that a number of them now leave the armed forces after their three years of service.
I know that the service term has been extended to four and perhaps even five years, and I feel that this is a good thing. In my opinion, the necessary steps should be taken to encourage young people to stay at military camps, and more especially those who go to university, since statistics establish that the majority of those who are trained in universities, thanks to subsidies from the Department of National Defence, leave the army afterwards.
Of course, this is not a total waste for the country, since those young people who come back to civilian life generally render to their fellow citizens services they might not have been able to render had they not received such training, thanks to the help of the Department of National Defence.
I heard a while ago the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) say that he is deeply concerned with the lower morale of our military men. He stated that they are worried about the future. I wonder, when he was responsible for the administration of the Department of National Defence, if he was so concerned about unemployment and the morale of the unemployed, because they could also be as concerned as the military people are today.
I do not think they have reason to be more afraid than any other Canadian citizens because through technological and economic progress they are affected in the same way as the factory worker who tomorrow will be replaced by a machine. As a matter of fact, I do not see why our soldiers' morale should be low. It should be as good today as it was yesterday because Canadian citizens do not see why the soldiers' morale could be good yesterday when they had guns but no ammunition. Would it be better to have more soldiers without guns and ammunition? I do not

think their morale can have been affected to that extent.
Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that the public is wondering in this connection, but I feel that every Canadian must realize that momentous changes are taking place. We are not in the thick of a shooting war and the present hot or cold war, call it whatever you want, is subsiding, and I do not see why the military would want to keep an army of 200,000 to 300,000 men for the sole purpose of giving them jobs.
Mr. Chairman, some people would like to see the total strength boosted to 200,000 from the present 120,000. As far as I am concerned,
I do not think that the reduction of the strength to 110,000 men, a reduction of 10,000 men, would affect the morale of the forces in general. As a matter of fact, I think the morale of our servicemen will improve when they know what action the Canadian government intends to take to maintain its military forces in Canada.
Will our military force simply be a police force, a peace keeping force, as some are advocating? Perhaps. In any case, if that is what is in store for our military forces, I think our servicemen would be happy to be informed about it, so that they may prepare themselves to play whatever role is to be assigned to them by the government and the Canadian people as a whole.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that with this Bill No. C-90, we are taking the first step that will likely result in a reduction of our military expenditures. Personally, I can but support this measure, because I always considered- and I never had any proof to the contrary- that the Canadian government was allotting too large a slice of its budget-26 per cent- to military expenditures.
There is hope that the amounts thus saved will be even greater in the future and that we can use them to bolster our economy in a more rational and practical way.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
During the course of the short debate we had on Bill No. C-90 last Monday a number of points were raised which had already been discussed during the hearings of the special committee on defence. The hon. member for York-Sunbury asked whether we considered the experience of other countries concerning integration of forces. Of course we did, Mr. Chairman. Steps have been and are being taken in many countries toward a more integrated organization. While it is true that other countries have not proceeded to the extent contemplated here, the trend is un-
National Defence Act
mistakable and in my opinion inevitable. As far back as 1945 testimony given before the United States congress was of some significance on this subject. General of the army Douglas MacArthur had this to say:
The great lesson for the future is that success in the art of war depends upon the complete integration of the services. In unity will lie military strength. We cannot win with only backs and ends. And no line, however strong, can go alone.
General Eisenhower, speaking of his experiences in world war II, said:
Unity of command in the field, so vital to our success, was not easily achieved. When war came at Pearl Harbor we had joint command. It was not until we surprised the enemy in North Africa that the first large scale example of unified command emerged. But it was a new device and there were many difficulties which yet remained to be overcome. All of these had to be met and surmounted during actual operations when lives were at stake. In my opinion, those difficulties grew directly from the traditional separation of army and navy, which is the inevitable outcome of the present organization of our military departments. Separation at the top necessarily fosters separation all along the line.
In April, 1958 in a message to congress, General Eisenhower made his recommendations:
Separate ground, sea and air warfare is gone forever. If ever again we should be involved in war, we will fight it in all elements, with all services, as one single concentrated effort. Peacetime preparatory and organizational activity must conform to this fact. Strategic and tactical planning must be completely unified, combat forces organized into unified commands, each equipped with the most efficient weapons systems that science can develop, singly led and prepared to fight as one, regardless of service.
The hon. member for Calgary North quoted the opinion of Air Marshal Curtis with respect to the discontinuance of the chiefs of staff of the single services, but I should like to quote from an even more senior air force officer. As far back as 1947 the former head of the R.A.F. bomber command, marshal of the Royal Air Force Sir Arthur Harris, wrote a book about his experiences, and in his conclusions he strongly urged one fighting force. He made the point that:
There is only one answer to this otherwise inevitable tendency in each of the services to get tied to a particular and invariably obsolete weapon, and all weapons are obsolete as soon as they are in use. There must be only one service: the survival of three of them at this stage in the development of armaments is wholly idiotic, and there never was any reason or need for them at any time.
That is the opinion of one of the most senior officers, who played a very significant role in world war II. Field Marshal Montgomery has, of course, stated his views on this matter of unification on a number of occasions. Talking

speechtext: Four, instead of three.

The hon. member said that the three services, according to Air Marshal Curtis, will be like ships without a rudder. Naturally I do not agree. I think they will be like ships with synchronized rudders, whereas sometimes in the past the three ships had their rudders set on a different course and were headed, one would expect, for quite different destinations. The waters may be uncharted, but I can assure hon. gentlemen that we have a compass, we know where we are going, and we will keep a sharp lookout for rocks and shoals on the course.
The subject of morale has been raised by a number of speakers, in particular by the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Calgary North. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that generally speaking morale in the armed forces at the present time is extremely high, particularly in the field. I have just completed a tour which involved visiting personally most of our units overseas, and I can assure hon. members of the house that their morale is excellent. They have no fear or apprehension whatsoever about their future or the future of the defence organization of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: In Cyprus too?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: In Cyprus too. I have never seen men with better morale than those.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Naturally when there is a reorganization of the scale proposed at the present time there is uncertainty, and particularly at national defence headquarters there is some uncertainty. We have said that we are going to do the job with fewer people. Inevitably there is some wonderment as to who the people will be that will be required in the future. I think the best way to restore the morale in this situation and to restore certainty is to pass this bill and let us get on with the job.
The organization is proceeding, planning is proceeding, and v/e will be in a position to cut
National Defence Act
over to the new organization within a few weeks of the time parliament passes this bill. In so far as the cut-over is concerned, I can assure hon. gentlemen that there will be no diminution in our effectiveness. The fighting units will be kept in the same high state of efficiency that they are in at the present time. Special effort is being made in this regard, and I have no doubt whatsoever that our fighting units will be just as effective as they have ever been and that there will be no loss whatsoever in this regard during the period of changeover. I can also assure hon. gentlemen that we will proceed just as quickly as we can without at the same time making too many mistakes. We want to get on with the job, and at the same time we want to make sure that each step is carefully thought out.
I would like to repeat for my hon. friend for Calgary North something that I had thought would be self-evident to everyone, but which apparently is not. That is, we will still have, as I have said before, squadrons of ships, squadrons of planes, battalions of men, and it does not matter whether these are in three services or one in so far as their operational effectiveness is concerned, their effectiveness will depend on their commanders. They are well commanded now and they will be in the future. But in order to effect the maximum savings in the organization and the administration, which the hon. member subscribes to and supports, and to have a military machine which is most responsive to the needs of the second half of the twentieth century and best adapted to combined military operations now and in the future, a single, unified force is the best answer by far; and I am sure that history will prove this to be correct.
I think no one should vote for this measure who has any doubt in his mind as to what we propose to do. It is true that the bill is limited in the sense that it merely replaces the chairman of the chiefs of staff and the chiefs of the individual services with a chief of defence staff. But let there be no mistake about it; we are going to reorganize national defence headquarters on a functional basis; we are going to try to make it responsive to the special circumstances in which we find ourselves at the present time. Then after that we are going to make whatever savings we can in other areas, in logistics, training and area commands so we will have the maximum savings available for the purchase of new equipment for our armed forces.

National Defence Act
We have stated categorically in the white paper-and this is at least our intention; this is our belief, and without it we would not be proceeding as far as we now have- that what we propose is a single, unified defence force for Canada, one which will be responsive, streamlined and effective to do the job now and in the future. In this regard we are, I think, ahead of some of our contemporary nations. But we have a responsibility to go ahead; we have an opportunity which is unique, and I think this house has a responsibility to pass the bill and make it possible for us to get on with the job, to show that we have the right solution, and to put it into effect just as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, it is rather satisfying to have the minister make a full statement in this house and in the committee, but there is one thing on which I should like to comment. That is that the minister has been sort of going back on the many eminent soldiers, sailors and airmen who have made statements previously in this connection. I may say at the start that I am wholly for this integration, but it is the lack of information that the committee had and the wonderment all through the armed forces that has bothered me.
As a preliminary question I would like to know from the minister about the proposed change in staff. Has any information been sent down through the three branches of the services setting out what possible changes may be made in personnel? How many have already passed into civilian life as a result of these proposed changes? I am wondering whether the minister could give me that information now.

I am trying to jibe this in my own mind. Was this part of the long term, ten year plan about which we heard? Were these initial 500 aircrew part of the ten year plan, or was

this something that was started ahead of time and just happened to coincide in timing with the change of staffs and the integration of the forces?

I think in fairness, Mr. Chairman, it can be said that the 500 reduction in aircrew was not directly related to the change in organization mentioned in the white paper. The surplus of aircrew resulted from two or three circumstances; first of all, from the build-up in personnel following the Berlin crisis, when a number of short service commissioned officers were re-engaged in order to provide additional aircrew if required. These were not required. Consequently they became surplus and have remained surplus throughout the months since that time.
In addition, some of the changes announced during the discussion of the estimates last year resulted in a reduced requirement for air traffic controllers and a few reductions in the establishment for aircrew officers. These made up the balance of the total. So as far as the 500 aircrew are concerned, although they have been retired at this time one certainly could have justified their being retired whether or not the proposed reorganization had taken place.

Mr. Chairman, I have no further thought on that point. Prior to the minister's statement just now, were the services made aware of the fact that this action was not a part of his 10 year plan but was just a general chopping off of 500 aircrew? Have they been made aware of the fact that it is not a part of the over-all plan he now proposes to bring forward, which may involve the removal of a great many more from the services? The minister says these 500 were signed on again for a period. Were they personnel who had indicated that they wanted to make the service their career? Were they taken on for a definite time, and have they been cut off before that time? What are the circumstances?
I think the minister can appreciate that I am concerned about the state of morale in the armed forces at the present time. It is all very well to say there is high morale among our troops in Cyprus, but that is a permanent force. It is all very well to say there is high morale throughout the services, but I have received a very different impression from correspondence and from talking to officers myself. It is my impression that the feeling is that what is being undertaken now is very bad for morale, and I am wondering how soon the services will be made acquainted with the situation. The minister mentioned the ship

which has a tri-service rudder, and I say all the more power to it. He also mentioned uncharted shoals. Just how many uncharted shoals is he going to have to navigate around?
I am asking these questions because of my concern about morale in the services, and because there are a great many men in all three branches of the services who may receive notice tomorrow or six months from now. To what extent are personnel acquainted with the fact that soon they may be removed from the careers in which they thought they had set themselves for the rest of their lives?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think there has been some uncertainty in respect of the reasons for the discharge of the 500 aircrew officers because of the timing. If any mistake has been made I believe it lies in the fact that this reduction perhaps should have been made several years sooner than it was. It could have been, and I can demonstrate that if you really want me to do so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the course of the minister's remarks he referred to the morale of the services, particularly on the continent and in Cyprus. I suggest that if the morale of these forces is not high, morale will not be high anywhere. Unfortunately I have not had the opportunity to visit these forces and see the conditions under which they are functioning at the present time. I will not deny the minister's statement with regard to the forces in those fields of operation, but I certainly do refute his statement with regard to the forces serving in Canada, on the basis of the conversations and communications I have had with members of these forces. They feel that a beginning could have been made by endeavouring to see what could be done with the existing organization before instituting the present plan.
I have my personal views in regard to the bill under consideration today. With reference to the quotations the minister read into the record from statements of chiefs of staff of previous years such as Bomber Butch Harris, I might say that I knew him personally because I had the privilege of serving under

National Defence Act
his command for quite a time, and I appreciate such views. I know fully what he had in mind, and so far as general thinking along these lines is concerned I would be inclined to be receptive to such views.
However, the one thing I must reiterate concerns the morale of the people currently in the forces. I do not believe that morale within the country is too high. I believe a clearer picture must be presented as to what the future will hold for the personnel in the services. The minister has just made an explanation of what will occur over a period of years. However, when the initial statement was made the public had the idea that an immediate saving of taxes was going to be made. Now we find that is not the case.
I had the privilege of returning to my home not too many weeks ago and speaking to a young man who was one of the 500 who had been discharged. He was lamenting his future and the future of his wife and family. Being a jet pilot in this age and being out of work is not the nicest thing that can happen. One does not change one's vocation in life without some misgivings or without a tremendous effort, and in many cases some sacrifice. The minister explained at great length that he felt the trend toward unification was inevitable. I must agree; I think that is most certainly the case.
Then we must ask ourselves, how do we start? Statements appeared in the press that so much money was going to be saved the taxpayers and that there was going to be a reduction in personnel during the course of time. The statement that so much money was going to be saved the taxpayers was somewhat misleading. We do not know precisely what the plan is. The white paper refers to the plan in general terms. I think it has been characteristic of this government to be rather misleading in this general field. If we co-operate with the other countries in the world with whom we must co-operate in the future, then surely we cannot expect we are going to save the taxpayers tremendous amounts of money. We should be given details as to where we are going to save it.
The general public should be told what the future plan might be. Are we going to reduce our navy by a number of ships? There are hardly any left now. Are our planes going to be effective in Europe when they are not at the moment, unless a great amount of money is to be spent on them? I suppose the army will finally fit into the picture when the bill is passed. Then we hear people in the country asking, what is going to be the

role of the militia? Will there be any role left for them? I think the minister should give us some of this information, and he should tell us what this is going to mean to the various provinces of Canada.
Recently we have heard about the extraction from the maritimes of certain areas of industry which are extremely important to that part of the country so far as the economy is concerned. Surely these proposals might also have a tremendous effect on this part of the country. Let the minister tell us what this is going to mean to the maritime provinces. This reduction in the forces could affect their economy. The minister has said it is inevitable and must take place. Let him tell us what the effect will be on the provinces. Let him tell us what the role of the militia will be in the future, so people who have devoted a large amount of time to this phase of our military organization will know what the future holds.
At the moment, as the minister is aware, representations have come from my particular part of the country, not from my constituency but from my part of the country in regard to the role the militia is to play. I am not going to mention any names because I am not referring to this to embarrass the minister or the government in any way. The people are wondering if the forces are integrated whether or not these units will be available for service to the country in time of need, and even in peacetime. I think we are entitled to have these answers. I hope the minister is prepared to give us this information before the debate closes.

speechtext: Carried.

speechtext:
It is obvious the hon. member for Port Arthur has little or no interest in this matter. He sits there and just mouths "carried" from time to time. However there are certain things I should like to indicate to the minister at this time. We are asking a number of questions at this time because after rereading the transcript of the evidence given to the committee I must say it was lamentable that the minister should withhold so much information. I was not present during all the committee hearings on this bill. However I have noted that there were many general statements made.
I believe this has become a general practice with the minister. When he was over here as the defence critic for the opposition, he used to cry to the heavens about the minister of the day being reticent in giving information. Well he was a chattering jackdaw compared to what this minister has

become. The minister has become a sphinx. I have never seen a minister who held back so much information that properly should be the property of the house or the committee. Naturally we asked for reasons. It is not sufficient for the minister to merely say "Well, I think"-or "We thought", or "Based on information we had we did this"-or did that. We want the reasons because this is a far reaching change. The announcement of it was accompanied with the greatest amount of ballyhoo this country has seen for many years.
The white paper referred to savings of $100 million on a ten year program, although the ten years was never mentioned in the white paper. There were some very carefully prepared news releases in this regard and the newspapers generally swallowed them whole. We saw headlines to the effect that million dollar savings were projected for national defence. How misleading. It is true that subsequently the minister said, after he was pushed into the position, that this would be achieved over a period of years. The impression remained with the public that national defence budgets were going to be reduced by a billion dollars over the next ten years. We knew this was not the case. The minister indicated later on, quite properly, that what he was trying to do was to get some money out of the administrative side to spend for new equipment. He has not got a monopoly on that. His predecessors were trying to do that as well..
The minister knows that the former member for Esquimalt-Saanich, when he was minister, indicated to the defence expenditures committee of 1960 and the estimates committee of 1958 how this problem was worrying the government and the senior officers of the department. Therefore there is no latter day discovery made by this minister. There is here an attempt to find some money by a reorganization of the command structure and it is accompanied again with a great deal of ballyhoo as to unification. There is great confusion between unification and integration.
You can have unification of command down to a certain point, but integration of forces means everybody wears the same uniform. You may call them A, B and C units; you may call them numerical units of the defence forces, but when they all wear the same uniform this is the ultimate in integration. The minister would be very wise to make a definitive statement on how far he is going to go. This afternoon he waffled on both sides of the question. He made a statement about a former
National Defence Act
president of the United States and he gave us a quotation.
Frankly all that General Eisenhower, the former president of the United States, referred to was unity of command, citing his experiences in the European theatre where they had a supreme commander allied forces, a unified command; but surely it goes beyond the limitation of any reasonable comprehension to read into General Eisenhower's words that every sailor, airman, and soldier would be in the same uniform.

speechtext: He said he would put them in the same uniform if he had his way. I think that is a direct quote. I can produce it if you want it.

But in any event, referring to some of the problems of morale, there is a great deal of merit in unification of command but I have some reservations about the methods being used by the minister. There is something to be said for unification of command, but I have very definite reservations as to this so-called integration if it means one force one uniform.
The hon. member for Calgary North referred to this when he mentioned the minister's statement about the artillery officer serving on a destroyer. He must know that in his position as minister people talk to him a lot less than they did when he was just the hon. member for Trinity, on the opposition benches.

speechtext: Just the opposite.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think the minister is wrong. He is patently wrong or else he is hearing those things he would like to hear, or the things people think he would like to hear, not the things that the men down in the ranks want to tell and do tell. If the minister thinks he is getting a true picture of the morale in the lower ranks, both at the officer and other ranks level, he had better get his head out of the sand because he certainly has it buried right there now.
At the beginning it was claimed that these proposals would result in a savings of $100 million, and would mean a reduction of about 10,000 in command personnel. Where is this $100 million going to be saved, and how? This is what 1 would like to know. It is not

National Defence Act
enough for the minister to say we are going to save $100 million. This whole program is so fundamental that the minister owes it to all members of the committee to say how he is going to do it.
I hope he has not just plucked this figure out of thin air because it looks nice and round. It has a resemblance to 100 days or 60 days. These are nice round figures and they look attractive, but surely the minister is working on something better than that.

The minister knows the Berlin crisis was in 1961. These aircrew were added as the result of a "beef-up" of Canadian forces from 120,000 to 135,000, part provided by the air force and part by the army and navy. Let us not hear this minister tell us that the number of these aircrew could have been reduced years ago by the previous administration. That is a lot of nonsense. The build-up only took place in 1961. If I remember correctly, it was in the latter part of 1961. Let us look back. The Berlin crisis and its consequences did not disappear overnight. Does the minister think one could have signed these men to serve for a period of years and then, six months later, said: The crisis is over; you are out. It could not possi-

bly have been done. There is no chief of air staff who would ever dare say to the government: I need another 6,000 or 8,000 men for six months. He would not be able to get past the minister if he had the foolhardiness to make such a recommendation. So the minister's statement was patently wrong. He could not give any reasons to back up his remarks, and he knows it.
The minister says we are moving forward one step at a time. He admits there are many questions which remain to be answered because events cannot be foreseen. But what steps has he taken to guarantee that he will not run into some real shoals or troubled waters, to use his own phrase, which would materially affect the integration scheme? How does he know he will not run up against a blind wall?
The minister may smile. I seem to remember when he was over on this side of the house, and when things were explained to him it was not done with any supercilious air. I am very serious when I am discussing this subject. There are problems which come to mind, and the minister has no monopoly on genius in the working out of a plan for the defence department. If the hon. gentleman can tell us what problems were envisaged and what solutions have been thought out to deal with those problems, then surely there would be a quicker acceptance of this plan. There are people, whether in the service or not, who foresee problems. This gives rise to doubts. The minister may have answers to the majority of them. Why cannot he give them to us? We were promised a full explanation in our consideration of this subject earlier but I have never read one which was more barren of information or which would lead us to the conclusion that the minister was doing anything else but asking the house to accept something which he had recommended.
As a classic example, there was a carefully prepared brief put before the committee by Mr. R. S. Malone recommending a variant tq the minister's proposal. It introduced a defence council within the hierarchy of command so that the chief of staff would not be the one and only adviser to the minister; the minister and the chief of staff were part of the defence council. I should like to refer to page 146 of the evidence before the committee where Mr. Malone, as reported, points out the dangers which might arise in connection with the proposal the minister is now making for the appointment of a single chief of national defence. I should like to hear the 20220-323
National Defence Act
minister counter Mr. Malone's argument. He is obviously not prepared to accept them. Let us have the reasons. His present attitude is not good enough. With the committee's permission I should like to read the first two paragraphs on page 146 and then a further paragraph reported on page 147 of the transcript of evidence.
May I also illustrate my point by the experience of Arthur Balfour one half century ago, when the British army was commanded by a single commander in chief. He held that having had no part, either personally or through his representatives, in the decision making process up to that point, the minister must either accept his experts' recommendations, in which case his superior authority is mere form, or he may enter into a debate on the pros and cons of the project and start afresh, in which case he has in effect rejected his experts' advice. Either way he has placed himself in a false position. The experts prevail over him, or he, a layman, overrules them, with consequent loss in time, effort, money and morale.
And I would add, confidence.
Assume for a moment that we could find a paragon of all the virtues to occupy the post of chief of the defence staff; in fact, a commander in chief. Look at the position in which he would be placed. All his professional associates would be junior to him, accepting his directions and orders and therefore not likely to challenge his decisions and no power to veto his projects.
Above this one, top expert or professional soldier are the amateurs or civilians-
And I am sure Mr. Malone in referring to them as amateurs or civilians did not imply anything derogatory, but the minister or the cabinet are not professional soldiers-
-in many cases not qualified or prepared to question his professional advice.
I think that is only fair comment.
It is hard to believe that such a top chief would not have some blind spots, some professional biases, some personal prides or fixations which could cause disaster. Surely the matter of national defence and the huge costs involved should not be subjected to such hazards. Certainly from an individual standpoint it is much easier to operate by yourself and be the complete boss and not have the problem worked through a committee, but it is not the individual interest we are thinking of here but the question of what is the right thing for the country.
In addition to that, I would point out one further difficulty, and that is that the two persons involved are to be very dominant personalities. There we would have a clash of which a summer thunderstorm would be but a pale shadow. Because if the minister is not such a dominant personality but his chief of national defence is a very dominant personality-and we have had some in this country; Canadian services have not been without them-then the minister will be a mere tool in the hands of the chief of national

National Defence Act
defence. On the other hand, if the minister is a very dominant personality and his chief of national defence is but a run of the mill type, then I think we are in the position where the minister would be also chief of national defence, to whom we could apply the old adage: "Why hire a watchdog if you are going to do your own barking?"
I come now to a further statement of Mr. Malone as reported at page 147 of the report.
For a minister to deal directly with individual military experts is to place both minister and expert in a 'false position'. The minister, he said, must either confirm the expert's decision, in which case his position as superior authority is a mere form, or he must enter into the reasons for and against and decide afresh, in which case the expert becomes superfluous. It is bad organization to have two men (the minister and the expert), one over the other, to do the same business.
Mr. Malone proposes that the defence council, instead of being an appendage and acting in an advisory capacity only-which is the proposal of the government at the present time-and composed of capable men who sit off to the side and are not in the chain of command, be replaced by a defence council presided over by the minister and composed of those same people but in the chain of command. Decisions shall be not those of the chief of defence made direct recommendations to the minister. The minister and his defence council, including the chief of national defence, shall formulate the decisions. The British have gone even further because they have introduced many more civilians into their defence council. I do not think I have to go into the details of that because the minister is quite well aware of which I speak.
Admittedly one may ask: How do you know their system is any better than ours? They have had experience of this supremo concept which is now being introduced and have got away from it. They are in the position of formulating a judgment decision on the basis of experience for the type of services they have had-ours are patterned on theirs-and they have decided that their organization is better suited to today's requirements. True enough, the minister has been able to quote from certain individuals who, based on wartime experience, feel they should have complete domination. Because who but himself would have been the number one in the eyes of marshal of the royal air force Sir Arthur Harris? I think with all due respect to Viscount Montgomery we all know who would have been number one there: He would have been. It is human to want to have it all under your own thumb. But surely to goodness the
[Mr. Lambert.)

Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to hear the minister's real criticisms of Mr. Malone's proposals. Those criticisms may be perfectly justified but for goodness sake let us hear them, because we have not heard them yet. Mr. Malone's comments are dismissed as though the exercise before the defence committee was a matter of form.

Mr. Chairman, I was and am a member of the defence committee. I attended I think as many meetings as did the hon. member for Vancouver East. I think I listened to the evidence with as much care as he did.
I did not avail myself during the committee meetings of the opportunity of making so many statements about things. I think the hon. member misconceives the purpose of a committee. Surely we know in this house that there is no such thing as a minority report; that if a report is submitted, it is the report of the committee. When the bill which is reported comes to the house for passing, that is the time when those hon. members who heard the evidence have a duty to make statements and comments on the bill. They are required to do this.
The statement I am going to make shortly is in my opinion in the nature of a minority report. This is my feeling about the report that was made and about the bill, and I do not apologize to anybody for making these remarks. If we are going to reorganize our defence organization, we are going to reorganize it for a long time; and if the house has not a day or two to listen to the comments and criticisms of the proposed reorganization, I think some people who loudly protest their great love for democracy know less about it than they claim.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why didn't you do it at the last meeting of the committee?
