speechtext:
Because this is the proper forum; this is where that criticism should be made. The purpose of the bill is commendable, in a sense, if we are going to make the armed forces more efficient and better operated, or if we are going to effect real and substantial economies. Those are commendable purposes, and they have been loudly proclaimed in headlines and press releases all across the country. But when we look behind the headlines and the press releases we begin to wonder if the efficiency and the savings are not much more apparent than they are real.
The criticism with regard to the command situation has been that with the chiefs of staff committee there has been no effective head to translate their views or to arbitrate between them, and that the Minister of National Defence has had to listen to too much
IMr. Lambert.]
divided counsel and too many different views and has not had a good system of evaluating those views. So we now have the proposal for a single chief of staff who will evaluate the views of all the various heads of the services and then present them to the minister. I do not know that this will improve the quality of the advice the minister will receive. Nor do I think it will provide the proper civilian evaluation of the views that the chiefs of staff or heads of the armed services put forward, and that the minister should have before he acts upon them. Presumably that was the purpose of the reorganization but I do not think that high purpose will be carried into effect.
We are told that this new set-up is going to cut down the number of people reporting to the minister and to the chief of staff. In the committee we were given a chart showing that there would be a chief of operational readiness, a chief of personnel, a chief of logistics and engineering and a comptroller general and were told that these men would report to the chief of staff. Two meetings later we asked questions about what the position of the heads of the navy, army and air force would be and we were told that they too would report to the chief of defence staff directly. Therefore instead of having a committee of chiefs of staff composed of four people we are now going to have a committee of seven. This seems to me to be the first indication that in the battle to cut down the armed services Professor Parkinson is going to win, and not the minister.
The minister is very popular in United States military circles at the present time. As a matter of fact, he has just become the man in the purple suit in a well known American magazine. I suggest that when he was reorganizing the services he might have looked a little closer at the recent reorganization in the United States department of defence. If he had he might have made provision for a small group of civilian technical advisers who could weigh and decide on the military hardware that we are talking about buying with all the money we will have for such equipment if we reduce the armed services by 2,000 people. We are going to need very careful evaluation of such equipment, and I think this was the time and place for the minister to provide himself with a small number of adequate and highly trained civilian advisers to advise him as to the value of the various weapons and defence systems that are proposed for us.
The other criticism I have of the new command structure is that it gives little or no

status whatsoever to the defence council. Indeed in the charts provided to us in the defence committee the defence council is not even enclosed by a solid black line but rather has dotted lines around it. Along with the rather casual attitude that the minister has taken toward the defence council, this indicates that little if any use will be made of it in the new organization and, indeed, there will be even less civilian advice for the minister in the future than there is now.
Brigadier Malone gave evidence before the defence committee. His main complaint about the Department of National Defence in the past has been that there is not enough civilian control. Indeed, he puts forward that very problem in his article in the Winnipeg Free Press of May 28, 1963, dealing with the suggested reforms in the Department of National Defence. In that article he said that too often civilian intervention has come too late in the decision making process to be effective, and went on to say:
A good deal of the authority which was once exercised by civilians-most notably during the war when each service had its own cabinet minister and deputy minister-has gone by default to the chairman of the tri-service chiefs of staff committee and to the individual chiefs of staff. In the absence of civil leadership these officers have been forced to make policy decision which in a democracy should really be made at the political level.
Under the present system, for example, it is not uncommon for the services to be working for months or even years on new weapons, spending large sums of money on investigation, research, design and so forth before seeking civil approval. By the time such a project reaches him for final approval, the Minister of National Defence faces the dilemma described by Arthur Balfour a half century ago, when the British army was headed by a single commander in chief: Having had no part, either personally or through his representatives, in the decision making process up to that point, the minister must either accept his experts' recommendations, in which case his superior authority is mere from, or he may enter in to a debate on the pros and cons of the project and start afresh, in which case he has in effect rejected his experts' advice. Either way he has placed himself in a false position. The experts prevail over him or he, a layman, overrules them, with consequent loss in time, effort, money and morale.
It would be very interesting if the minister would describe to us in detail how under the new organization he proposes to make good the lack of civilian control and supervision at an early enough stage. We have been given all sorts of glorious figures about saving $100 million and cutting 10,000 people from the armed services, and told how we are going to be able to buy a lot of new weaponry with all the money we are going to save. But I wonder whether we are going to save it.

Each time one questions the number of persons who are being cut from the armed services the number is less than it was the last time. Each time the cost of living goes up, and surely it has gone up fast enough even for my friends opposite in the last year, the savings are reduced and we are able to buy that much less new weaponry.
The other ground to which the minister presumably would turn would be better buying and more efficient administration. In all his discussions he has been curiously reticent about the position of the Department of Defence Production in relation to the new organization of the Department of National Defence. I suggest to him this is where there should be some real reorganization and where there are some real savings to be made. On this fascinating chart with which we have been supplied we have a chief of logistics and engineering. Under him will come design, development, test, evaluation, inspection and quality control. In the six years I have been a member of the house those are exactly the things the Department of Defence Production has been supposed to be doing with regard to ships, airplanes and all other types of military weaponry. Is the Department of Defence Production going to be dropped completely or are we just getting more duplication here?
I could give the house some examples of places in which savings could be made because of bad administration in the past. I have to mention the Avro Arrow. I am not mentioning it from a political point of view because that is aside from the administration of the department completely. One of the things that forced the decision on the Arrow was the absolutely fantastic and uncontrolled costs in connection with the Arrow. What is the minister doing to change the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production in order to reduce the type of waste that occurred in connection with the Arrow?
Then there is the Starfighter. The decision to acquire the Starfighter was a political decision in the sense that it was a decision that had to be taken by the politicians. We hear now that it will have to be redesigned and that will cost another $50 million in order to make it work. These are administrative decisions made by the experts and no politician could possibly know about the design of the Starfighter. What is being done to make sure there will not be $50 million more wasted on the next weapon we buy? This is where the minister could make some saving.

Then I should like to refer to the naval drawing office. We find that the pumps on H.M.C.S. Provider do not work and that the hangars are not big enough to hold the helicopters. No politician designed those. No politician knew about them; he had to accept the advice of the experts. Let the minister tell us how he is going to correct these situations. Is he going to bring the aircraft procurement and naval procurement sections of the defence production department into his department? Is he going to put them under civilian control? This is where some real savings could be made, rather than in the lopping off of 2,000 men from the armed services.
These are the questions to which the committee would like answers. We deserve answers before passing this bill. We do not need any long statement about the good will of the minister. We need to know how he is going to exercise effective civilian control. How is he going to do it? How is he going to make our procurement more efficient, not just putting things on a chart, but what are his plans? These are the things we must know before we can have any hope of more efficiency in the armed services.

I get quite upset and irritated by statements from members of the smaller parties who endeavour to cloak themselves in purity by trying to give the people of this country the impression the official opposition is endeavouring to obstruct the government. The official opposition is merely trying to do its job by endeavouring to secure the information that we should have before decisions are made about the legislation before us.
Certainly, this is the only thing the hon. member for Vancouver East endeavoured to accomplish when he spoke today. I, for one, am most anxious to discuss this bill and ask the minister certain questions to which I hope I may be able to secure answers, in an effort to understand better how I should vote on the measure when that time arrives.
I was impressed, Mr. Chairman, by the remarks of the minister concerning morale

in the forces. Being a member from Nova Scotia, I am especially impressed because a large part of the Royal Canadian Navy is located there. If the minister feels that morale in our forces is excellent, I would suggest he take a trip to Halifax and talk to some of the men in that arm of the forces. I have found no high morale in the navy, and I do not think anyone else has who has been speaking to anyone in the navy. As the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg says, the situation is just the reverse. These men do not know where they are going and that is the reason we are asking questions today. We want them to have a better appreciation of what is happening. I see no reason why we should not continue to ask these questions over and over again until we get the answers. This will give personnel in the armed forces an opportunity to know what their future is, whether they are going to be employed in the navy, for instance, or on civvy street.
There is another matter which has only come up within the last few days to which I must refer, so that the people in the mari-times generally can appreciate what is happening. Ever since this government has taken office we have seen substantial cut-backs in our armed forces, in our defence contracts and in everything associated with national defence. It has been a case of cut, cut, cut and nothing more nor less. They talk about alternative programs, but we never seem to see them. We are most anxious to see them, or if we are not going to see them we are most anxious to know that so we will have some appreciation of what we are going to have to plan for in the future in order to replace what has been taken from us.
Today I asked the Minister of Industry to indicate to me what the plans are for the future in so far as defence contracts are concerned. He is not yet ready to tell the people who are unemployed in my constituency or in the constituency of Halifax. I certainly hope he will be shortly and that he will be able to indicate a long term program that will allow us to prepare ourselves for whatever is to come in this regard. I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence this question: Is there a change of policy on the part of the government in so far as defence establishments are concerned in the maritime provinces? May we still expect the preference, if you want to call it that, given by the former administration which resulted in the people associated with defence establishments in the maritime provinces having some certainty

as to their continued association with these defence establishments? This is an area that is beclouded. It has been beclouded since the minister started to make statements of policy-relating to the cancellation of the general purpose frigate program, the suggested elimination of the reserve base at Summerside, the elimination of the naval repair depot at Point Edward and the elimination of the radar station outside Halifax.
I would like to know what are future prospects in the field of new equipment for the navy. Are the shipyards in our area going to be given the same type of attention that they received in the past? We have suffered from the cancellation of almost $100 million in contracts.

paper the associate minister-I am subject to correction on this-stated it cost approximately $85,000 to train aircrews. I suggest the minister should calculate this amount of $85,000 for training as against how much it will cost the treasury to let these trained personnel go.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I know the committee has been waiting to hear from the minister of defence. He has sat in his place in supercilious silence except for one or two observations. The committee wants to hear from him an answer to the various questions which have been raised. It deserves that answer. The minister seems to have adopted the philosophy of so many of his colleagues-I can think of the Minister of Finance and I can think of others, also-who rushed into the house with a plan, and, when it came up for consideration, found it had to be altered or changed, or was a dismal failure.
All of us are in agreement that action should be taken to bring about economy and efficiency in the armed forces. The minister enunciated his plan some months ago in a white paper. However, what is before us is simply the question whether or not there should be a unified command, in other words whether the chairman of the chiefs of staff

committee and the chiefs of the naval staff, general staff and air staff should be done away with and replaced by a chief of defence staff. It was mentioned this afternoon that following discussions which had taken place in the special committee there was no place in this committee for consideration of the matters which had received the vocal attention of the defence committee. I have read the evidence given before that committee. I have read it from beginning to end and, having read it, I cannot but be left in a position of deep uncertainty as to what will result from the plan which is before us in the amendments now being considered.
The purpose is efficiency and economy. The minister has said economies will be effected. He has not placed before us anything in the nature of evidence to support the generalization that the result will be beneficial economically. Certainly what has become apparent since he became minister is a deep sense of uncertainty and fear among members of the armed forces in every part of this country. They cannot understand the purposes and aims. They have not been given a full and complete elucidation of the minister's ideas and those of the government. It has simply been a case of generalization accompanied by failure to go into particulars which would give those who serve at least some reasonable approximation of what will transpire, of what will happen to them, and what benefits are likely to flow as a result of unifying the command. Certainly experience in the past, going back to 1904 in the United Kingdom when the Esher commission made its recommendations has never established that benefits commensurate with the hopes of the minister will be achieved. This follows from the consideration given to the question of unified command not only in the United Kingdom but in the United States. I know great stress has been laid on the economies which would be gained by cutting out duplication of services, duplication in command, duplication in procurement, in supply, and so on. But when we come down to examining what has taken place in the months since the white paper was brought in we can only fear for the future of our armed forces in Canada, particularly in the field of morale.
I said a moment ago that the armed forces have not been taken into the confidence of the minister. He has not given them the facts, he has simply generalized. Now he comes before this committee, after hearing evidence in the defence committee which was anything but unanimous among the witnesses produced 20220-324
National Defence Act
before it, and would have us believe that the initial step is one of placing one man in command-a service superman who will discharge the responsibilities which were formerly discharged by the chiefs of staff of the various branches of the armed forces. Certainly we are entitled to have more information in this regard.
The uncertainty of the position was recently revealed in a meeting which took place in Washington. Much was made of the joint meeting between the United States and Canada. Great hopes were expressed as to what would take place. When the ministers returned from Washington they spoke in fulsome terms. The Canada-U.S. cabinet committee on defence had not met for four years, so the Prime Minister decided that it would be most beneficial if that committee were to meet. We have to depend on press references for information as to what happened. Mr. Bruce Phillips of the Washington bureau of the Hamilton Spectator said this, in part:
The first meeting in four years of the Canada-U.S. cabinet committee on defence.. .created the impression that once every four years is far too frequent.
The meeting apparently was a gross waste of everybody's time.
I am surprised at that, with the minister there and with the other ministers present at the meeting.
By all accounts it consisted mostly of exceedingly general discussions which pointed nowhere in particular.
I am not surprised at that. One does not expect ministers to be any more pointed in their observations abroad than they are at home. The report goes on to say:
But the question arises whether such meetings have any value if people leave with the feeling that they have wasted their time.
Then some of the matters discussed are referred to, and apparently the minister gave a most interesting dissertation on a unified command; but nowhere does the report indicate that anyone was overwhelmingly in support of the explanation he gave. The report continues:
It is a subject of continuing interest in the defence department, which has tried unification...
The report might be summarized by saying that the members of the committee drifted away with nothing but a few listless assurances to give the matter of joint defence and production sharing some thought.
That has been the difficulty here, Mr. Chairman. I see the minister sitting in a pose with his right hand holding up his jaw, and

National Defence Act
his finger in the best Karsh fashion, forbidding all information to the house. He is decorative, attractive and appealing; I am prepared to say that of the minister, for whom I have a very large measure of respect. But his sitting in that pose I can only say means it is to take the place of information, apparently.
We should like to know what is being done. What is the evidence which came before the committee to which allusion was made this afternoon? The first point is that the proposal calling for a single defence chief must be taken in context with other proposals made by the government, which were summarized by the minister on May 26 before the defence committee. He ended up with a recommendation to replace the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, and the three service chiefs. He was then asked by the hon. member for Greenwood to give a detailed analysis of the proposed savings, and the evidence then concluded pretty quickly because the minister could not give any such information. What the minister has done to date is to promise economies which have consisted in transferring expenditures from one department to another and in covering them up, whereas in point of fact he has not been able to bring before the house and the country any record in this regard.
What about the single defence chief? Is it appropriate in a democracy to concentrate all power and responsibility in defence matters, subject of course to approval, in the hands of a single individual? Will one person necessarily be familiar with the technical and military requirements relating to all three services? However estimable such a person may be who is designated to this position, this kind of concentration of authority has not worked anywhere in the world. There will be the blocking of direct contact with the minister from the heads of the three services. Information will be funnelled through a single channel. Where is the coordinated long range defence policy which was promised on May 8? Can it only be achieved by one person assuming these powers? To say that it cannot be achieved except by putting all power and authority in the hands of one person is contrary to the experience of any military power in the democratic world. Certainly people are beguiled by this plan. It is doing something. Economies are going to result. Five hundred aircrew are removed; they are not even part of the plan apparently, we learn today. Only the other

day a young man was in conversation with one hon. gentleman in this house. He had been nine years in the force. He is an authority on jet propulsion and is a jet pilot. But he is out now. Where does he go? He says he got no notice but was just told he was out. Is this a system which will promote sound morale? Is this the kind of action to be given to those who joined the armed forces with the expectation of other treatment?
Mention has been made of the evidence given by Air Marshal Curtis. I am not going to repeat what has already been placed on record, but there is one matter not yet answered by the minister or by anyone else which will have to be answered by him. It concerns savings proposed in the white paper of $100 million a year. Air Marshal Curtis said, as reported at page 163 of the report:
I understand this will call for a reduction of roughly 10,000 troops in order to make that possible because integration itself will not come anywhere near to doing that. Also, I would think it would take probably a reduction of closer to 20,000 troops to make a saving of $100 million a year possible.
What he said has been placed on the record. He said that our services are going downhill both in regard to morale and in regard to spirit. Then Air Marshal Curtis, who is fully acquainted with and knowledgeable of the position in the United States, went on:
I was in Washington two months ago and the report I got from the senior officers there was that although this was an interesting experiment they were too polite to say what they thought but they are not going to attempt it.
I should like the minister to tell us, when he was in Washington meeting with this joint Canada-U.S. cabinet committee, those men of experience, what they thought of this plan, because I hope he told them more than he has told us.
Sir, the serious, searching and penetrating criticism from a former chief of staff, reading it objectively, cannot be disregarded, based as it is on a great deal of experience in both war and peace. The minister would simply brush it aside. We want to know the answers to these things. We want more than sophisticated silence; we want more than an attractive pose on the part of the minister. We want him to place before the house and the country the evidence that he has. Certainly General Macklin's views, too, were quite interesting when taken alongside the optimistic hopes expressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding the troops sent to Cyprus. The hon. member for Vancouver East said we should not go into these things.

I wonder how many read what General Macklin said in regard to Cyprus:
When we sent a battalion to Cyprus a few weeks ago, there was not enough airlift for its heavier equipment and so it went into that hostile island half equipped and half armed and waited two or three weeks for the rest of its armament and equipment to come by sea.
What a risk that was to subject Canadian soldiers to.
We mentioned some of these things.

speechtext: This is categorically denied.

We want to hear some categorical denials, Mr. Chairman, not from a seated, posed position but from a standing position in which the minister will review what has been said. General Macklin said as well:
The third defect is that there are absolutely no reserves of any kind anywhere behind the formations of the regular army. If the NATO brigade got into a battle it would be into a manpower crisis in no time.
These are things that are concerning Canadians. This was evidence that was given before a committee. Is it not about time that the minister, if he is able to do so, has the knowledge to do so and the advice to do so, placed before the house and the country the facts? Certainly the placing of omnipotent power in one person will not meet situations referred to by Air Marshal Curtis and General Macklin. We ought to have this information because, as I said earlier, this government's approach in connection with defence has been an uncertain one. There have been many promises of what would be done; there has been a white paper that generalized- but these things have been followed by no effective action.
All we are asking is that the minister shall place before the committee the facts. What efficiency will result from this unification of command? What controls will there be, other than the committee that is being set up, over what I would call the omnipotence of one person? What is being done on behalf of those who are serving in the armed forces, to diminish-yes, abolish-the destructive, demoralizing concern of the armed forces? Simply to say "cut" for the purpose of being able to argue that effective action is taken, is not sufficient. What are the economies that will result? Those are questions to which we have a right to answers. The committee met. It is obvious, as the hon. member for Vancouver East said, that the committee had the fullest information. However, I submit that the house will not accept his conclusion, that this information covers in the detail it should 20220-324J
National Defence Act
the various questions that I have raised, that are merely by way of summary of the views expressed here this afternoon by one hon. member after another.
We are not here for the purpose of endeavouring in any way to embarrass the government. What we are here for is to endeavour to assure that when experiments are being undertaken, experiments that have no basis of experience, this house and the country shall receive fuller information than it has received in the past. Experiments there will always be; but I think that when an experiment like this is being placed before the Canadian people, unsupported anywhere in the free world by the approval of experience, the questions asked by hon. gentlemen this afternoon deserve an answer, and the fullest answer that the minister can give.

speechtext:
I should like to raise some more questions. I should like to have answers to the questions I raised the other night when we were discussing this measure. With regard to the problem just mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East, may I say that I was a member of the defence committee last fall and I objected to some of the things that were in the report of that committee. We were not permitted to bring in a minority report, but when I raised the point at the final meeting of the committee it was quite obvious that there was not unanimity in that several members were dissatisfied with items that appeared in the report. However, as a committee we could not show the various items with which we disagreed. So the report was made public.
I have read all the evidence presented to that committee. I noted that quite a number of members of the committee raised questions which were unanswered by the minister, and raised objections as they proceeded with the discussion of the bill as it was before them. I can quite understand why those members, having stated their objections once, did not bother to repeat them when they came to the last allotted day for consideration of the matter; but it certainly does not follow from a reading of the evidence that there was general agreement with the bill.
I am surprised at the casual attitude of the Minister of National Defence, and I use the phrase that the hon. member for Simcoe North used only a little while ago. That is the impression the minister is creating now. He has taken a casual attitude toward a very serious matter. The importance of national defence is something of which we in Canada are apprised and the subject merits more than just a casual attitude.

This minister has been in office almost 15 months. I ask him: What has come out of that 15 months of casualness? We have heard about study groups, seminars and appraisals of this, that and the other thing. But what has actually come out of that 15 months in office? Is there greater efficiency in our armed forces at the present time than 15 months ago? The answer I give is no. There is less efficiency than there was 15 months ago.
The minister has reduced the complement of ships in the navy. He wiped out the Sabre jet squadrons in Europe before the 104's were prepared for effective action. Even now that air division in Europe is not fully armed. He has reduced by two squadrons the Voodoos in Canada and has not armed the remaining Voodoo squadrons as he promised to do. What has he done for the army? What changes in the army has he made in these 15 months? Where is the mobile equipment he was talking about? He has not even provided a nuclear missile for the Honest John battery about which he made so much noise approximately 18 months ago.
The efficiency of our armed forces has declined under this minister and we cannot get from him the answers that are essential. There is a lack of confidence in the minister. He talks boldly and says that under the proposed reorganization the armed forces will be responsive. I do not know just what he means by that. He says they will be streamlined. This is supposed to encourage everybody to think they will be better forces. He gives us no evidence of how that will be brought about.
How can we have confidence in a minister who carelessly talks about an artillery officer, as the hon. member for Calgary North mentioned today, and says, to use the minister's words, that he "may find himself quite at home with a naval gun after a brief familiarization period", as if he could serve acceptably on board a ship just because he was a trained artillery officer on land? What confidence can we have in a minister who, in response to a question in the house last week, informed the house that a camera on a reconnaissance plane was a conventional weapon? This is the type of answer we are getting from the minister, and the confidence that may have rested in him 15 months ago has rapidly dissipated.
His responses to questions in the committee, his responses to our questions in committee of the whole house on the bill, have been inadequate. When we came to take up the bill the other night after it had been

reported back from the defence committee I had to press him to get up and make a statement. He took about a minute and a half or two minutes, although I had asked him to give us a report on the type of evidence that was reported to the committee, general criticisms, if any, of the bill, and let us know what had happened. The minister dealt with none of these things. He simply made general statements and confined himself to stating, as found at page 4846 of Hansard of June 29:
This bill implements government policy set out in a white paper on defence and is the necessary first step to bringing about integration of the three headquarters leading, we hope, to increased efficiency and a reduction in overhead expenditures.
That is all he said in the committee of the whole house when the bill was taken up the other day. That is not good enough. As he was urged to do today, the minister has to define what he means by integration and unification, and I propose to deal with those two points later. He has to tell us exactly how he expects to achieve a reduction in overhead expenditures and at the same time, which is his chief responsibility, retain the fighting effectiveness and efficiency of our armed services.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I will resume at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I started at just five minutes to six with a few introductory remarks and my intention was to give the minister the supper hour to collect his thoughts, return here to the house and give us answers to questions. I propose to give him a few more minutes to assemble his
National Defence Act
ideas, and I express the hope that when I have finished or perhaps when someone else has spoken, the minister will make a comprehensive statement on his plans for the future. Just before six o'clock I read out his basic statement which he made the other night, in which he expressed the intention of the government to bring about integration of the three headquarters, leading to increased efficiency and a reduction in overhead expenditures.

I realize that he has been placed in a strait-jacket by the Minister of Finance since he has been limited to a billion and a half in money to support the three services and provide equipment for them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is still too much.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Now that amount of money may be too much. Someone in the far corner, I guess it was the hon. member for Lapointe who is constantly interrupting from his seat, has said that. It is open to question whether it is too much. It depends upon what you are getting for your money. When we consider the expenditures of money in which we were involved in the first and second world wars and in Korea, perhaps we are well advised to maintain our defences at the present time and spend some money that way rather than be plunged into a conflict in the future unprepared. Under those circumstances we are aware, from our experience in the past, that a great waste of money occurs.
However, within the limits the Minister of Finance has set for the Minister of National Defence, he is now attempting to divert some of the money to the purchase of equipment. If he can do that without impairing the effectiveness of the services, we are not in disagreement because modern equipment is an essential. I read in a newspaper not so long ago that the minister said he was embarking on a 60-day period of decision. I am not sure what date that started, but we will be watching very closely to see the effect of the 60-day period of decision because we have been through that once before. This is where we came in, in the movie. I wondered at his temerity in stealing from the Minister of Finance and from the Prime Minister a

National Defence Act
statement such as that. In this 60-day period of decision he is going to place orders, he tells the production industry, for military equipment. We will watch closely to see whether or not the services are kept in balance in the expenditure of this money or whether one is preferred over another.
We will be particularly interested in seeing whether the army, which has been doing a major portion of the active work during the last several years, is given the mobility it requires. I want to deal with the vagueness of the minister's ideas concerning his plan. On May 8, when we were discussing the bill, the minister was talking about the various choices he had before him, and he is reported as follows on page 3066 of Hansard:
The third alternative, which was the one finally-adopted, was the integration of the armed forces into a single unit.
Then on page 3188 of Hansard for May 12 the minister is reported as using these words:
I think it follows logically that once the high command has been unified and once the armed forces of Canada are organized on a functional basis rather than along traditional service lines the complete integration of the armed services will follow as a natural evolution from this change in organization.
So, he told us what he thought, and again he used the word "integration". In the white paper on which he bases his whole case, page 19, he uses these words:
Following the most careful and thoughtful consideration, the government has decided that there is only one adequate solution. It is the integration of the armed forces of Canada under a single chief of defence staff and a single defence staff. This will be the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.
The minister has been asked what he means by his use of the words integration and unification. This afternoon he quoted at some length from various prominent leaders in the second world war, who used words which he considered bolstered up his case. MacArthur spoke about the complete unification of the services. Eisenhower spoke about unity of command in the field and about one single, concentrated effort. Harris, the celebrated "Bomber" Harris, talked about one fighting force and one service, and Montgomery said that the committee system was unsuitable in a fighting service.
These are men of distinction and it is important to get their points of view. I notice in the defence committee report that Brigadier Malone interviewed some of these people after the war and had conversations^ with them as to their ideas about organization of the services.

General MacArthur, fighting the war in the Pacific, was faced with amphibious operations and he had to use combined forces, air, sea and land forces, in order to land on the various islands and establish a position. He found that it was a difficult operation unless the troops were trained for that type of combined work. The United States marines had more experience than the army units and set the pattern for the island hopping that was characteristic of the Pacific campaign. I think when General MacArthur was talking about unification of the services he was thinking in terms of amphibious operations where it is absolutely essential that the three services work together.
Similarly, when General Eisenhower was talking about unity of command in the field he was thinking of combined operations leading to landings in north Africa, Sicily, Italy, and on the beaches of Normandy where the navy, army and air force had to work closely together to achieve effective results.
I do not doubt for one minute that Air Marshal Harris was thinking in terms of a unification of command among the three services, although his activity was largely in the air, and much doubt has been cast upon some of his planning and his direction of strategy in the massive bomber assaults on Europe. It is the opinion of many military experts that under better direction some of the war effort of England and the United States might have gone into aircraft for close support of the army rather than be devoted to bombers.
General Montgomery was quite familiar with combined operations and realized the value of them, but it is not necessary to unify the three services into one single service in order to get successful combined operations. We saw enough of that in the second world war to understand what it means.
Even within an army itself you have combined operations, because not only have you infantry and tank formations but you have artillery and engineers, all of whom have to be welded into one striking team, and if you can combine with that striking team tactical air support then you have an effective fighting land formation. We have had the experience of that. It was done without putting all the personnel into one formation or one service. That is why we fail to understand what the minister is talking about when he leaves the impression that in time he will end up with just one service.

It is obvious to anybody with any military service at all that you cannot interchange as readily as that in the fighting formations. You may make changes in the administrative tail of an army, air force or navy. You can have the trained mechanical assistance, the electricians, the ordnance people and the supply people-there can be a change there, but how you can interchange people in fighting formations escapes me entirely. It just cannot be done. We had enough difficulty in the second world war effecting good co-operation between tanks and infantry, and between air force and infantry formations, to realize the problem.
What does the minister mean by his integration of the services? Is he going to put everybody together in one uniform? Are they to be interchangeable? How does he have an effective fighting force? His job as the Minister of National Defence is to have effective fighting forces whether they are on the sea, in the air or on the land. Judging by experience I would say this is best done along the lines familiar to us now, with good training on combined operations and with the high command thoroughly familiar with the three services. These are the people who carry the fate of the troops in their hands, and if the high command has knowledge of the functions of the three services then you can get proper results, but why you would need to go beyond that I do not see.
Some of the expert witnesses who appeared before the defence committee dealt with some of the factors I have been talking about. The other evening when I was talking on this bill I dealt at some length with Brigadier Malone's evidence before the committee, dealing with a study of the Esher report, and I was astonished today to hear the minister say that the chief recommendation of the Esher report was the setting up of area commanders. Having read the Esher report I could not reach that conclusion at all.
As the hon. member for Calgary North pointed out, and as has been mentioned by others, including myself the other evening, the Esher report was brought in to correct the deficiencies that had been shown up in the British army under the supreme commander in chief idea. With experience in two or three wars, and with experience in the Boer war- the South African war-the decision was reached that a change should be made. The Esher report advised and parliament finally adopted a council system whereby the commander in chief was not responsible for everything that went on and whereby the minister,
National Defence Act
with four military advisers and three civilian advisers on the council, was able to get better and more complete advice than from one supreme commander. This is what we think the minister should be doing here, rather than reverting to a system which was tried many years ago and found wanting. In 1904, when the Esher committee reported, the system was changed in England, and it was also changed in Canada, because the people here read the same report.
One man who was very largely responsible for the implementation of the Esher report was Balfour. He subsequently was prime minister of the United Kingdom. He served as head of the cabinet committee on defence. Later, when there was a change of government and Asquith became prime minister, Balfour was invited by Asquith to sit in on the meetings of the committee on imperial defence. Subsequently when a coalition government was formed he went to the admiralty, and later he became foreign secretary. So he was a man of vast experience whose interest, during a large part of his life, lay in this question of defence.
His sponsorship of the findings of the Esher committee was decisive. A council was set up and functioned with considerable success from then on. Had it failed in world war I and world war II, it would have been changed by now. But it was not. I suggest therefore, that our own experience plus the experience of other nations should be drawn upon in these circumstances, and when the minister tells us that the chief recommendation of the Esher committee was simply to appoint area commanders he shows he is not familiar with the report, for otherwise he would not have made such a statement.
I have here excepts from that report which I propose in the few minutes remaining to me to put on record for others to study. Part II of the report reads as follows:
For the first time in the long annals of war office reform its intricate problems have, we believe, been approached from the point of view of war rather than from that of peace. The scheme we have laid before you is based upon the consideration that the preparation for war is the primary object of a war office, and that no military organization can be sound in time of peace unless it is applicable to the necessities of war.
I should like to interject here that, much as we hesitate to talk about war, our defence department nevertheless exists for the purpose of giving us adequate assistance and protection in time of war. It is not a peacetime organization. So anything which is done by

National Defence Act
way of reorganizing the Department of National Defence must be done with a view to what would happen in case of a conflict. We may be able to manage, having adopted the minister's idea of a supreme commander, when we are faced only with operations which Canada is obliged to perform, or agrees to undertake as so-called police actions in connection with United Nations peace keeping operations. But these activities are not war.
So in the light of our experience from the first part of the century Canada must look to the future. We cannot be sure we shall not be involved in some conflict where the lives of men are at stake, and if the lives of men are at stake there must be efficient handling of the service organizations. That is when the great test comes. Have they the equipment? Are they trained? Are they ably commanded? Or are their lives to be wasted? We have seen enough of that in the past to make us cautious about making mistakes in the future.
The committee report continues as follows: Bearing this principle constantly in mind, we have proposed-
(a)	A permanent nucleus for the defence committee, in order to ensure the continuous consideration of defence problems and to co-ordinate the naval and military forces of the crown. We regard this proposal as the keystone of the whole structure of reform.
(b)	An army council for the higher administration of the army.
(c)	The creation of a trained general staff, which is one of the most pressing military needs.
(d)	Divorce of administrative from executive military functions.
(e)	Complete decentralization of administrative work.
(f)	A thorough system of inspection.
(g)	Financial changes, in the interests of sound economy, and increased responsibility of the military administrators of the army.
(h)	Division of duties within the war office, to prevent overlapping to minimize reduplication of effort, and to ensure the smooth and rapid dispatch of business.
Those are the effective recommendations of the Esher committee report and it is on this basis that the reorganization of the British army was carried out after 1904.

Mr. Chairman, this is becoming an exercise in futility. Here we have the Minister of National Defence occupying a very important position in the government and bringing before us a bill which he claims is the first step in his program of integration of the forces. He has had the most tremendous press build-up all over the country that I have seen. Yet we cannot get from this minister answers to legitimate and serious questions.
May I tell the Minister of National Defence that we are not treating this problem lightly. The question of the national defence of this country is of vital importance. It is an expensive proposition. From the point of view of the taxpayer we want to know whether the money is being properly spent. We have thousands of young men in the services. Behind those services there is a great tradition extending back throughout the whole life of this country. We, the Canadian nation, have put forth great efforts in wartime and are putting forth great efforts in peacetime. The minister has come along and is going to change things, and we want him to give proof that his proposed changes are for the betterment of Canada's national defence. We want him to give us proof that there will be no deterioration in the combat effectiveness of our services.
As I said a few minutes ago, I am not thinking in terms of a peacetime army. You can have a peacetime army which will never be called out for active service. But our experience in this world has been that Canadians have been called upon to go to war. A
National Defence Act
lot of people do not like that word, but that is what we have faced four times within the last 60 years. Canadians have been called upon to go to war, and they get killed in warfare. If the services are efficient, fewer men get killed; that is what it amounts to. If they are inefficient, lives are wasted.
What we are asking of this minister is this. He must demonstrate to us without shadow of doubt that his proposed changes will maintain unimpaired the fighting efficiency of our services. He must show us that his proposed changes will increase their effectiveness. Otherwise what is he about? Is he just building up a little empire for himself? Is he trying to make great claims for himself? This is too serious a matter for that. We are now talking about the national defence of this country, and as I pointed out from the Esher report, when you are talking about national defence you are making preparations for the war that you hope will not occur, but which may occur and for which you have to be ready. We are saying to this minister that his proposal for a supreme commander in chief is likely to weaken the effectiveness of the fighting services, and he has not given us any proof to the contrary. We are pointing out to this minister that some of the plans which he has underway, as the hon. member for Simcoe North I think it was pointed out, will enlarge the responsibilities of the former chief of the general staff instead of reducing them, and will make his work even more complicated.
The other evening when we were discussing this bill we pointed out from the evidence given by Brigadier Malone, who was quoting from the report of the Esher committee, the inherent dangers in having a supreme commander in chief who may become the dominant figure in the defence services of this country and put the minister in the shadow. Or if there is a conflict of interest between the two men, one of them has to go. If one has to go it is damaging, on the one hand to the government, and on the other hand to the services. Why is the minister launching on this uncharted sea? He himself is not a man of vast experience, yet he will not tell us who are his advisers who have put him on to this particular course, and he will not give us adequate reasons for the changes he proposes. Because we treat this matter as of the utmost seriousness, we are insisting tonight that we get adequate answers from the Minister of National Defence,

National Defence Act
and I will now give him an opportunity to give us some of those answers.

National Defence Act Mr. Hellyer: I stated this afternoon, and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has disagreed, that the chief recommendation of the Esher report was to put into effect a system of area commanders. The reason I say this is that it was the only, or at least the major, recommendation which has persisted, which has lasted, which has stood the test of time. The army council which was recommended and established then to have independent powers has had its powers eroded. My hon. friend, being an ex-minister of national defence, is thoroughly familiar with that. The chief of the general staff was then only one among equals, though the senior member of the council, through the passage of time had his powers augmented until he became in fact the chief executive officer of the army, and the council in fact became subordinate to him. This happened years ago, and I am surprised that my hon. friend is now suggesting an organization which went out of style years ago, presumably on the basis of the experience of skilled men in the army both in the United Kingdom and here in Canada. I think it is interesting, if not symbolic, that hon. gentlemen opposite would recommend an organization which is based on conditions that existed in 1904. I think they would be well advised to turn their attention to the conditions which exist in the world today and see if they cannot apply their ingenuity to a solution which is adequate to the second half of the 20th century, which is the time period we are really most concerned with at the moment.
Hon. gentlemen would not expect me, I am sure, to comment on the detailed plans in respect of bases, and so on, in the maritime provinces, because that would be out of order on this bill. Therefore I will try as best I can to confine myself to the considerations of the bill that is now before us. I have given the reasons for integration many times.
I have stated that in my opinion it would not be possible to implement a co-ordinated defence plan for Canada without integration of the high command. I think that is reason enough in itself. Under the present system, with three independent chiefs and three independent services, I do not think that any minister could in the long run implement a co-ordinated defence plan. That is my opinion based on my experience. In order to implement a plan over a period of time which is co-ordinated and objective for all the armed forces, I believe it is necessary to have a unified command. That is the reason that one has been recommended.

National Defence Act I have also stated, and I am firmly convinced that it is the way to achieve the maximum savings, that only with a single unified command can you effect the maximum savings at all levels, from headquarters in Ottawa to area headquarters, logistics support, engineering, training, supply. This can only be effected with a single administrative organization in charge of the three armed forces. We have tried integration the other way and there have been some derogatory remarks about it on the other side of the house. We have had some areas of integration and there have been some real problems. One of the reasons there have been real problems is the continuation of three independent services and the fact that it was possible for any one service to implement a veto or to put obstacles in the road of implementation of recommendations put forward by the personnel members committee or by the minister to integrate a particular area of our defence forces.
In respect of morale I have stated that generally speaking morale is good. Certainly it is good in our overseas forces. It is good amongst our field forces here in Canada. I have stated quite honestly that there is some uncertainty particularly at national defence headquarters, and I have also stated that in my opinion that is inevitable. You cannot have a major reorganization along the lines we have proposed without a feeling of uncertainty. This cannot be avoided. You cannot have a new policy involving the employment of less people in national defence headquarters without having this feeling of uncertainty which exists at present.
The way to end the uncertainty and to improve morale at national defence headquarters is to permit us to get on with our job. Our planning has proceeded to the point where we have done as much as we can do until this bill is passed, and every day that goes by now without the bill being passed aggravates the situation which exists at national defence headquarters. It not only aggravates the situation in respect of morale at national defence headquarters but it results in the postponement of potential savings involving tens of thousands of dollars. So my recommendation to the committee is that we get on with the job, refer the bill back to the house, give it third reading and make it possible for us to go on to the next step, to provide that certainty which I know the armed forces would like to have and to effect the savings which I am sure all Canadian citizens are interested in our achieving.

In each of the forces you still have a separate board of some sort. The minister has either not looked at the organization existing there, which has produced unification of command as I have already indicated on two or three occasions, or otherwise he has not understood it.
He made a statement a few minutes ago which is completely at variance with the facts and which the merest glance at the organization chart for Great Britain, without reading

how the system works there or studying it, is enough to convince anyone of the true facts. If you look at this chart you will see the secretary of state for defence and under him the minister for the navy, the minister for the army and the minister for the air force. Then there is the defence council consisting of the secretary of state for defence, the ministers for the three services, the chief of the defence staff and the chiefs of staff of each of the services, the chief scientific adviser, the permanent undersecretary of state and the deputy minister. This is the same sort of situation we have had here. Under this you have the chiefs of staff committee and the defence staff. It is all one staff as far as the operational end of things is concerned. You have the defence secretariat, the defence scientific staff, and then you have the admiralty board, the army board and the air force board all reporting directly to the defence council where the ultimate authority resides.
To say that this totally disappeared years ago and that we are talking about something that went out of date many years ago just shows a lack of knowledge of what the present organization is in Great Britain, which was only completed in the last two years and is really just getting into operation properly there.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend is confusing the reference I made to the army council with the defence council, which I was not discussing.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

National Defence Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

We are accusing this minister of going back to an outmoded system. I cannot understand why he is doing it. Ever since the 1904 report the British system, and for a time ours, was organized with a council in authority and not a supreme commander in chief. Now the minister, without advancing arguments, is reverting to an outmoded system. He is the one who is living in the past. We want him to come into the present.
To reinforce what the hon. member for Calgary North has said, let me read come of the things Brigadier Malone said to the committee. This will be of guidance to people who are seriously interested in this subject.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Brigadier Malone drew attention to the new British system and a chart is displayed on page 142 of the committee report. This is what he said, as reported on page 143:
I would like to draw your attention to the fact that there they are not attempting to do what we are doing here. They are attempting to centralize the command structure only; they are not trying to unify the forces. In Britain three ministers are being maintained under a single secretary of state. Directly under the ministry level you will notice there is a defence council, not a chief of defence staff. The chairman of that council is the secretary of state himself.
This corresponds to our minister.
The secretary of state must participate; he must be part of the decision; he cannot say, "The experts told me this"; he must be part of the decision and he must answer for it in parliament; and either he or his deputy must attend.
Then, they are going to have the members of the three services, but in your case you will not have the three services but you will have heads of branches, that is the G branch, the administration branch and the supply branch-call it what you will, I prefer in my own chart to simply call them administration and supply as they are simpler this way.

National Defence Act
Subsequently, Brigadier Malone produced a chart giving his ideas on how things should be organized. I should like to quote one more paragraph:
Now then, the defence council breaks down into three services, in the case of the British plan, but it does not go to chief of staff, chief of air council, admiralty board, on anything, it goes to a board. At the bottom of the British chart you see the admiralty board, the army board and the air force board. In the old days it used to be called the army council, the air council and the board of admiralty. They are still maintaining that this board will have the authority, and not a single man.
The minister says to us, let us revert to the old system of 60 years ago under which they had one single commander in chief. Let us not adopt a modem plan of having a council where there are seven people or so on that council who have the authority and must bear the responsibility. Why the minister wishes to revert to an outmoded system escapes me entirely. He will not tell us from whom he got the advice. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the minister should either give us a fuller explanation than he has given or he should revise this bill because he is running into trouble. We are trying to help him. We want him to avoid difficulties with the services and with all the paraphernalia that goes with the services. Surely, sir-

I was called out this afternoon while the minister was making a brief statement. I did not hear him directly, but I understand he gathered from my remarks that I was under the impression that senior military officers were, or could be made, directly responsible to parliament. He wanted to correct me and inform me that it was the minister who was responsible to parliament. I am sorry if the minister misunderstood what I asked. Last Monday, when this matter was last under debate, I mentioned the subject and to clear the matter up I should like to quote a sentence. I said, then:
The main question is this: Whether parliament will have, in effect, one individual, in this case the chief of the defence staff, who is to be answerable to the minister for the defences of the country,

or whether you are to have a council each member of which is appointed as a result of legislation and whose duties are specified in that legislation so that he can be held responsible if a particular phase of defence is not up to par.
All I was saying was that in most defence acts, and in our defence act at one time, there was a council set up and the provisions specified the membership of that council and what their responsibilities were. This is all I was recommending. Of course, there was no suggestion-it would be absurd under our parliamentary system-that any military officer should be reporting directly to parliament.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REPLACEMENT OF CHIEFS OF STAFF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not wish to press the minister any further but I shall record my great disappointment that he will not give answers to this committee. I charge the minister with failing to carry out his duty as a responsible minister of the crown. We are entitled as members of parliament to get information from the treasury benches. We have asked legitimate questions and fair questions of this minister. He sits in arrogant silence and refuses to answer. I have never seen an example of this, to this extent, in my experience here in the House of Commons.
All we are asking this minister is a reasonable response to reasonable requests. Basically we have said to him: Advance your arguments for attempting to put into effect an outmoded system which was found wanting in the past. But he will not give his arguments. In the second place we have asked him to explain what he means with regard to unification and integration of the services. Does he intend to wipe out our three fighting services and attempt to make one out of them? If so, what is the experience and the evidence on which he is founding such a decision? Surely the House of Commons is entitled to an answer, and why cannot we get one from the Minister of National Defence? Of course we appreciate his attitude. We have seen it now, month after month. He thinks that nobody on the opposition side knows anything about defence. I recall asking him if he wanted to get advice from the special committee on defence last fall. He said: No, I do not require advice from the committee. Yet the committee was supposedly set up to give him advice. This is the type of arrogant attitude which the minister has shown, and it is regrettable.
What we fail to understand is why the minister, as a responsible minister of the

crown, will not give answers to these questions. He sits silent with regard to the unification of the services. He has told us at other times, or his words lend themselves to this interpretation, that he intends to have just one service. Frankly I do not see how that is possible. I do not see how it is possible to combine naval, air and land services into one force. Men are not interchangeable to that extent. I can understand-and I have seen this in actual practice-a combination of services working together effectively. That has been the experience in various wars, particularly in the second world war. But what does the minister mean? Is he wiping out the infantry regiments and the tank regiments which have a tradition behind them going back almost a hundred years?

speechtext: No.

This silence of contempt is a shocking attitude to adopt toward parliament and, once again, I call upon the minister to give us a comprehensive statement in answer to our legitimate queries. National Defence Act
A few moments ago the hon. gentleman said there had been some changes brought about at the level of the lower echelons but that each service maintained an effective veto over how far the process went. Does he intend to do away with that veto, and is there to be an elimination of the individual services consequent upon the elimination of that veto? These are matters which should be clarified. It would be simple for the minister to tell us what he thinks about this. After all, it is he who is proposing the changes. Let him who proposes the changes prove his case. This does not consist of making merely the flat statement: I think this is a better way to do things. If the minister is confident that what he proposes is correct, then surely, nothing should deter him from putting forward reasons for his attitude. They are not bound up in some great mythology. I think the motivation is simply this, to get the maximum amount of effective forces in the highest state of readiness for the least amount of money.

Mr. Chairman, this has been an interesting debate, one which recalls to my mind events of not so many years ago. Questions have been asked this afternoon and evening which parliament has a right to have answered. The minister has proceeded throughout the afternoon, with the exception of one or two more or less unimportant contributions, to remain silent and to follow a course of action which has been his since the time he became minister. One cannot but recall that no minister has since the year 1956 followed the course which has characterized this minister today and on previous occasions. His attitude is one which is in keeping with what took place in 1955 and 1956. It is that of a minister who refuses to give information; who regards his silence as something which is commendable; who refuses to furnish parliament with answers to reasonable questions; who sits and smiles and sneers when asked questions which are of pre-eminent importance to Canada.
I am not going to press him any further to answer these questions. I am simply going to point out that it is this attitude of insolent arrogance which brought about in 1957 a change of government. It is an attitude on the part of a minister who refuses to answer, having brought in legislation which will effect tremendous changes in the life and future of many thousands of Canadians in the armed forces. This is a minister who has been questioned by two hon. gentlemen who have occupied the portfolio of defence. The minister's answers have been proven-those which he gave-to be totally out of consonance with the facts and the course respecting defence organization in the United Kingdom. This is

an example of the arrogance that so often in the past was the characteristic trade mark of those who now sit opposite.
I can only point out once more that the retribution that comes to those who refuse to answer is recorded in the history of our country constitutionally and on more than one occasion. It is an attitude on the part of ministers-and there are only a few of them sitting opposite who have this attitude-of treating parliament with contempt and with a cavalier disregard of the rights of members of this house. I look back over the years to some former ministers of defence. I think of Ralston, I think of Power, I think of Macdonald during the days of war. I hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce applauding because he knew them. Those ministers answered questions when they occupied the position of defence minister.

We fully expected from this minister, who has received such glowing press reports from time to time-inspired, I presume, by his own office-some first-class exposition of his policy with regard to national defence. On the one or two occasions when he did attempt to make an intervention, we pointed out his error, his lack of knowledge of the subject matter.
Mr. Speaker, this bill deals with the setting up of a supreme commander in place of the present chairman of the chiefs of staff committee and the various chiefs who have been serving under him. We are now to have one single commander for the armed services of this country-a system outmoded, outdated which has been proved beyond peradven-ture to be ineffective; a method used in the past by the United Kingdom, which resulted in unnecessary losses to that country in warfare.
With that type of experience behind the minister, if he has any knowledge of the past at all, he has persisted in foisting upon this country this outdated, outmoded and inefficient system and he is going to hand over to one single individual the control of the armed forces of this country under the supervision of the Minister of National Defence. I have indicated already tonight that as far as we are concerned, we have no confidence in this Minister of National Defence; and if we have no confidence in him, what about the services generally?
