speechtext:
If we are to have these catcalls and cries of "carried" by people who have no knowledge of military matters, I am prepared to wait for silence in the chamber. It does interfere with debate and makes it difficult to continue. We will probably hear from some other people pretty soon Whose opportunities were not grasped at the time.
As I was saying a few minutes ago before the interruption, the purpose of the bill is to replace the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee and the chiefs of the naval staff, general staff and air staff with an authority who will be charged with all the functions, powers and duties of the persons being replaced, to be known as the chief of the defence staff. That is the main purpose of the bill, and the other clauses of the bill are

consequential because of that particular amendment.
We have endeavoured to point out the weaknesses of the system proposed by the bill. We have endeavoured to show that putting one man in supreme command is a weakness. We have suggested that it would be better to have a council charged with responsibility and that with such a council, consisting of a certain number of military advisers and a certain number of civilian advisers given power and not simply acting in an advisory capacity, two things would be accomplished. First, civilian control over the armed services would be maintained, which is essential under our democratic system. Second, the minister would have military advice over and above that which might be proffered by the supreme commander alone.
The idea of having a supreme commander is attractive to some minds and has been and still is used in some countries. But in some countries where there is a supreme commander in charge you get revolutions and undue influence on the part of the services with regard to the government of the day. This is something to be avoided. That is why in countries with lengthy democratic experience civilian control is emphasized, strengthened and maintained.
In considering this particular bill our suggestion was that it would be far better to have a council comprised of military and civilian representatives with authority to reach decisions with regard to a great many problems. The problem of procurement of equipment, in which taxation is involved, the problems of recruiting, mobilization of manpower, accommodation, transportation for troops, the allocation of equipment and money among the navy, army and air force, all these things are better decided by a council of military and civilian advisers working together with the minister than by one supreme commander on his own initiative.
It is all very well to say that an advisory council is being set up and that this council will provide the military and civilian advice requisite under the circumstances. That is entirely different from having a council charged with responsibility. If such a council consists of seven members, those seven members, acting somewhat like a cabinet, have to take collective responsibility for the decision they have reached. This would provide a more sensible method of looking after our national defence problems than the one man idea, because in that council you would

have the benefit of the experience and advice of seven or eight people.
Under the bill now before the house the contrary will prove to be the case. The supreme commander will reach his decisions based, of course, on consultations with others of lower rank. He will consult with civilian advisers within the department, but in the final analysis he has to make a decision and give his advice to the minister. Then you can have a conflict between two people, the supreme commander and the minister. The minister is responsible to cabinet and to parliament and has to accept the responsibility.
We have tried to point out the dangers inherent in a system where you have two people who are obliged to agree or else one or the other has to go. What position will the supreme commander be placed in if his advice to his minister is that, for example, there should be a vast increase in one of the three services and the minister is of the opinion that this is wrong, and one of the other services should receive greater attention? What happens? If the supreme commander is adamant, what does the minister do? On the one hand, the minister becomes just a satellite of the supreme commander and has to take his word for everything. On the other hand, if the minister enforces his will on the supreme commander and tries to get him to do something contrary to his military experience, the supreme commander either becomes a tool or puppet of the minister or he resigns and you have an upset in the system.
I know it has been argued that the committee system is unsound, but this is not a committee system that we have been advocating. It is a council; it is a meeting of minds just as in the cabinet. It is a relatively small council but it carries responsibility and gives instructions to the forces.
Attention has been drawn to the fact that a supreme commander may have undue influence on subordinate commanders. He may tend to surround himself, and this is natural and characteristic of human nature, with men of like mind, men who have the same ideas as himself. Under those circumstances how can you get a proper decision? There is plenty of experience both in wartime and between wars to indicate what happens when people in military forces get fixed ideas. I can give one or two examples which come readily to mind. In between the two wars we continued in Canada cavalry formations. Yet in the first war the cavalry, except in Palestine and in the very early days in 1914, was a useless
National Defence Act
weapon. The cavalry massed on the front for the breakthrough which did not occur, and when the Canadian cavalry brigade did get through on August 8 and 9, 1918, they were mown down. About 80 per cent of the force was destroyed by machine gun fire in just a few minutes.
Well, that is one example of what happens when people have fixed ideas. The people who were in control in between wars still pinned their faith on horse cavalry and neglected the new arm, the tank. Canada went into action in 1939 and 1940 ill-equipped for modern warfare. Supposing you get a supreme commander whose mind is cast in a mould that favours an outdated method of conducting warfare, an outdated method of training troops or an outdated concept of how a war should be fought. We will run into trouble. The frailty of the human mind is such that this is what might well happen, and we have seen it happen in the past. It can be observed in a reading of history.
I well recall another example of the fixed military mind or the inexperienced military mind. At the conclusion of the second world war a meeting was held in London with regard to an armoured personnel carrier. Three officers of the Canadian army were summoned to the meeting in London to put forward a proposal as to the type of vehicle which should be used as an armoured personnel carrier. Within 20 miles of London I was resident in a camp, and I was the only officer with the rank of lieutenant colonel who had used an armoured personnel carrier in action, but I was not consulted. Three officers who had never seen one in action sat down at a meeting to determine what an armoured personnel carrier should be like. This is the result of the fixed military mind which sometimes cannot see the woods for the trees.
We have seen the situation here in Canada. Only now are we getting to the point where we will have an armoured personnel carrier for our infantry forces. Despite speech after speech I made when I used to sit in the back row of this house concerning the necessity for an armoured personnel carrier in order to save the lives of infantrymen, it is now 1964 and we still have not an armoured personnel carrier.
This is one of the problems that arise in the field of national defence. I have just given you examples from my own experience. I expect similar examples to be drawn from the navy. Supposing there is not a

National Defence Act
nuclear war, but another war in which transport vessels have to be escorted across the ocean. Supposing the man in charge is against the convoy system. We have been through that in the history of the last 40 years. This was the trouble in the first world war. There was no effective convoy system introduced against the threat of the submarine because of the fixed military mind among the admirals. The danger that you run into, therefore, is this danger of having one man in complete charge. If his mind is inflexible, if he is determined on his course, what can you do? It is for this reason we suggest that instead of one supreme commander there should be a council, mixing military people with civilians and retaining civilian control which is essential, because in a democracy the civilian control is paramount. The armed services must be given direction from the civilian authorities.
We are opposing this bill, Mr. Speaker, on the grounds that it represents a throwback to earlier times. It is bringing into Canada a system which was rejected many years ago both in Canada and in the United Kingdom. We think it is absolutely unsound. The minister, intent as he is on reform, should have moved more slowly, one step at a time. If in the Department of National Defence there were too many committees and subcommittees, too much duplication of effort, why did he not try the system suggested by Air Marshal Curtis of giving more authority to the chief of staff or make the chairman of the chiefs of staff, along with the other chiefs of staff, into a council and give them the authority? He could have tried it out to see how it would go. Oh no, this minister says this is a new idea. Not having read history and being bereft of any practical experience, he seizes upon this idea of a supreme commander and now is attempting to foist it upon our armed services.
He says that this is just a step toward unification of the services. I fully appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot deal with that particular subject but I refer to it because the minister has indicated that is his intention. This is step No. 1, the supreme commander, and then the unification of the services. We feel that in this instance the minister has made a serious mistake. We have expressed our regret that he has been unco-operative. I now believe his lack of co-operation is due to a lack of knowledge of his subject. We regret that he failed to answer our questions and to explain what is in his mind with regard to his proposals for 
the future. It is our intention to oppose this bill at the third reading stage.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy for the opportunity provided by this debate on third reading to join my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) in making a few observations. Unfortunately, it was not possible for me to be in the house earlier in the day. I think the subject matter is of sufficient importance that we should take advantage of this opportunity which is not usually taken on third reading to add some further comments.
I cannot join in the criticism of my colleague who has indicated that during the course of the debate today many questions were not answered in connection with this important subject of the reorganization of the Canadian armed forces. However, there were general questions of policy that remained unanswered, and which I would like to bring to the attention of the house at this stage of the discussion.
First, as we heard during the debate, this is not a new method or technique of organization so far as the experiences of other countries are concerned. This leads to the question that having been tried in other countries, particularly a country like the United Kingdom with its wide ranging military responsibilities, is this sudden leap forward in reorganization in the best interests of efficiency at this critical juncture in our nation's history?
The bill before us, which provides for a supreme commander of the armed forces, is more concerned with the public relations aspect of reorganization arising out of the recommendations of the white paper on national defence than it is a realistic approach to reorganization in the interests of manpower economy as well as actual fiscal economy. When the white paper was produced I was one of the first to criticize it as more of a public relations document than as a concrete effort to meet the difficulties of Canadian armed forces organization, difficulties which are not new, because up until recent years, except in times of war, Canada's military formations have pursued a rather disjointed policy.
The whole idea of integration emerged gradually in recent years. It began actually with the advent of General Pearkes to the ministry, when he started a trend toward integration which was designed as a new approach to reorganization. Now suddenly in this bill we have abandoned the gradual ap-

proach and in one fell swoop, at least according to the public relations aspect, we are trying to unscramble all the errors of policy, or lack of policy, which had given rise to the difficulties of armed forces organization down through the years.
There has been a tendency on the part of the government of Canada to downgrade the importance and significance of our armed forces in peacetime. This was the pattern between world war I and world war II, and it was followed to such a disastrous extent following world war II that when the crisis of Korea came upon us Canada had to embark suddenly upon a crash program. In fact this was the name given to the program of recruiting and reorganization that took place at that time by the then minister, Hon. Brooke Claxton. He referred to the crash program that was necessary in order to gear the Canadian military formations to the demands of the struggle in Korea.
I suggest that the proposal before us has somewhat of the unplanned crash aspect that the hurried unplanned activities to meet the Korean crisis had back in 1950. But it goes even further than that. One of the reasons why we have had such extreme difficulty and extended debates on defence during the fifties and the sixties is because of the lack of consistency in policy until the advent of General Pearkes to the ministry. This lack of consistency created a perpetual crisis in defence planning, particularly in the air force sector of the Department of National Defence.
We had some momentous debates in this house when this party formed the government, when the first gradual move towards integration took place, when Canada embraced the NORAD system of defence after a long period of delay and hesitancy on the part of the previous Liberal administration. The Liberal party then in opposition were highly critical of even the gradual approach toward integration of the service aspects of the armed forces. They were particularly critical of some of the reversed decisions with respect to planning for the equipment needs of the air force arm of Canada's forces. I refer, of course, to the noisy debates that took place at the time of the cancellation of the Arrow program.
Why did it become necessary to cancel the Arrow program? It was simply because of the crash type of planning referred to by Hon. Brooke Claxton, which became necessary to meet the demands of the air force. All the resources of that rapidly growing air industry in Canada, A. V. Roe at Malton,
National Defence Act
were suddenly diverted from peacetime pursuits, such as work on the jetliner, and concentrated on producing the CF-100, which became quickly obsolescent and was superseded by the CF-105, because no careful long term policy planning to meet the hardware needs of the air force had ever been undertaken.
The former Conservative government was strenuously criticized for its decisive action in this regard. I am not going to revive the debate at this time other than to point out that decisions of that kind became necessary because there had been no consistent policy planning to meet the needs placed upon Canada's armed forces immediately following world war II. Not only did it become necessary, to meet the Korean crisis, to institute crash programming, but I can remember in the years 1946 and 1947 when Canada was asked to participate in the occupation of Europe, the Liberal government of that day had decimated our armed forces to such an extent that we were not able to take our rightful place, a place that Canada had merited by reason of her outstanding contribution in world war II. We were not able to take that place because of this tendency to proceed on a hit and miss basis in meeting our peacetime armed forces commitments. It seems to me that the desire of successive Liberal administrations has been to reduce our spending on the forces to an irreducible minimum, even though it came down from $2 billion in the early fifties to $1>
billion due to the economies of the former Conservative administration.
I feel that this bill which would place a supreme commander in charge of Canada's armed forces is putting the cart before the horse. Before we have a supreme commander to carry out the organization as outlined in the white paper I would suggest that the government and the Department of National Defence should proceed to more specific planning in the direction of integration than is outlined in the white paper. I presume that some of the policy questions which were asked this afternoon and which remain unanswered were related to some of these specifics which still have not been explained by the Minister of National Defence.
There is one further aspect of this subject which concerns me. It seems to me that having embraced the NORAD concept of continental defence-and I would remind the house that it was a Conservative government which first accepted the principle of continental responsibility for the defence of

National Defence Act
North America-the new administration is going to the extreme pole in this aspect of armed forces reorganization. They were hesitant to embrace the NORAD principle early in 1956 and 1957 because to a certain extent it meant the surrender of national sovereignty. But now-and this is the only possible manner in which the new top level structure of the armed forces organization as contemplated by this legislation could possibly work-it seems to me that we are surrendering the sovereignty of Canada's forces to another power.
Let me by way of illustration refer to the so-called Bomarc debate. This was an even more furious debate both in the House of Commons and across the nation than was the debate concerning the cancellation of the Arrow program. The essential point at issue in the Bomarc debate was the loss of Canada's ultimate sovereignty over her own armed forces. When I hear of the gradual disbandment of fighter squadrons such as 410 squadron, and more recently 414 squadron, it seems to me that this planning will reduce Canada's air force potential to complete dependence upon United States airpower. The essence of the Bomarc question was simply this: Is Canada to maintain ultimate control over her own armed forces or is she to surrender this control to a foreign power? We are reduced to three fighter squadrons-three all-weather fighter interceptor squadrons and two Bomarc squadrons armed with atomic warheads. It is still not known whether Canada has ultimate control over those warheads. It seems to me that these policy decisions have already been taken by the government in anticipation of the structural reorganization contemplated in Bill No. C-90 and if the government proceeds with this reorganization at the upper echelon of the officer level, the supreme commander will merely be accepting the policy put forward by the government which has already acquiesced in the ultimate and final control of the Canadian armed forces by the government of the United States.
This is a question which concerns other countries besides Canada. For example in the British House of Commons just two weeks ago the government came under fire from the Labour opposition for accepting submarines armed with the Polaris missile in much the same way as the former Liberal opposition criticized the Conservative government of the day for its acceptance of the Bomarc without the final decision concerning the atomic warhead. The defence of the

British government, as was the defence of the Canadian government during that debate, was: The warhead is American; the Polaris is American; but ultimate control of the missile will remain in the hands of the British government. It seems to me this is the crux of the matter and it is of fundamental importance to Canada as a nation, because if we are surrendering military sovereignty it is a long step toward surrendering political sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday morning, July 3, as recorded in Hansard at page 4992, I drew the Prime Minister's attention to the very firm announcement he had made on Tuesday, June 30, at page 4907 of Hansard, with regard to the debate on the flag. As hon. members are aware, that announcement was

in definitive language to the effect that the debate on the flag would be continued until it had been concluded. Accordingly I asked the Prime Minister whether he would not give the house an equally firm assurance that the legislation respecting the Canada pension plan would be continued in this session until it had been concluded. As hon. members will recall, the Prime Minister's reply was that the Canada pension plan would be introduced in the fall part of this session and that it would be proceeded with, but that further than that he could only say that he hoped it would be concluded.
My point in asking for this matter to be transferred to this overtime period is surely quite clear. I think it is a very reasonable request which we are making on the floor of this house that there be at least as definite an assurance regarding the Canada pension plan as has been given with respect to the flag.
I would point out that the assurance about the flag debate is that it will be concluded before the house rises for a summer recess. All I am asking with regard to the Canada pension plan is for an assurance that it be concluded before the session ends; and it begins to look-I am not jesting; I am making a serious prediction-as though the session probably will not end until Christmas.
I think we have the right, Mr. Speaker, to have an equally definite assurance with regard to the Canada pension plan, and I hope that the house leader, who I understand will be answering on behalf of the Prime Minister, will give that assurance tonight. As hon. members know, we in this party-and I think this is true of members of other parties as well-would like to see the Canada pension plan brought on sooner. We would like to see it brought on this summer. Indeed, that was the original plan. But as announced by the Prime Minister when he spoke about the business of the house last Tuesday night, it is a fact that we have had negotiations respecting the business of the house to be dealt with during the summer weeks. The results of those negotiations, as I say, were announced by the Prime Minister last Tuesday night, so it is clear to everyone that dealing with the Canada pension plan has been put off till the fall.
It is an open secret that one of the reasons it is being put off is because it is taking time to draft the legislation in its revised form. In other words, the bill is not yet ready. I am accepting the result of those negotiations; indeed, I must accept them because I took part in them. But I am concerned as to 20220-325

My fear is that if we do not get moving with the Canada pension plan, if we do not receive a firm assurance from the government, it is one of the pieces of legislation which may very well be put off until next year.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, we were going to have it last year, but it was put off until 1964. It has already been put off a couple of times this year. I say that in view of the importance of this piece of legislation, in view of the place it occupied in the government's election platform of 1963, it is not good enough for us to be told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) merely that he hopes it will be dealt with at this session. I think we have the right to be given the assurance that it will be proceeded with, and proceeded with to a conclusion; and we should have an assurance that is just as strong as that which we have had with respect to the flag. We know that the Canada pension plan after second reading will be referred to a committee. That would be a good time to resume the debate on redistribution. But first of all let us get the Canada pension plan moving this fall, and let us have the assurance now that it is going to be stayed with until concluded; let it be just as firm an assurance as we have had with respect to the flag.

subtopic: CANADA PLAN-REQUEST THAT CONSIDERATION BE CONTINUED TO CONCLUSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one thing that I must first make note of in this house is the interest of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken in the matter of the Canada pension plan, and the other matter which I must note, in due justice to him, is the genuine character of the interest which he bears to the question. I may assure him that the sincerity of the government and the government's desire to proceed with the Canada pension plan as early and as definitely as possible is just as genuine and intense as his own.
The government is, as the hon. gentleman noted, at the present time completing the drafting of the bill in certain of its technical aspects. In view of the discussions which have taken place in this respect and certain modifications which have been agreed to for the purpose of assuring that this country once and for all will have a nation-wide Canada pension scheme, of course certain adjustments had to be made and they must be reflected, especially the technicalities involved, in the actual drafting of the bill.
I can assure this house that it is the firm intention of the government to do everything possible so that the final stage of the legislative process with respect to this legislation can be achieved and completed before the end of the current session in the fall. But the Prime Minister of course could not state a date the other day. In this connection I want to say that the government does not have the same measure of control over the continuity of the legislative process with respect to the pension bill. It will, as the Prime Minister said, be sent to a committee and will have to go through all stages. But, given the full assistance and co-operation of the house at each stage, the government undertakes to obtain the completion of the legislative process with respect to the Canada pension plan before the end of the session.

subtopic: RICHELIEU WATERWAY
RICHELIEU WATERWAY
subsubtopic: STUDY BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I asked the Prime Minister if the government was going to proceed shortly with the Richelieu deep waterway project.
In 1961, the Conservative government asked the boundary waters commission to make a survey in order to carry out, if

possible, the Richelieu deep waterway project. That study must be over now, I am quite sure.
It would be of importance to connect Montreal and New York through the Richelieu river, which is the shortest navigable waterway. The route between Montreal and New York would be shortened by 1500 miles through that waterway, instead of going around by the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Atlantic ocean. By using that means of transportation, Canada would save $125 million a year.
Since Canada is ready to pay in full expenditures connected with its troops in Cyprus, without any help from the United Nations, I wonder why the government is delaying the implementation of that project which is of vital importance to our country's economy.
I would like to know if anyone is against it and why the work is being postponed.
Referring to the newspaper Le Devoir for September 19, 1960, I note that the hon. members for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), both ministers now, met with their colleagues from the Quebec legislative assembly and approved a resolution asking Ottawa to carry out an investigation, which was ordered by the Conservative government. The government was also asked to proceed with the deepening of the Richelieu river in the fall of 1960.
Appearing before the international boundary waters commission and speaking on behalf of the chamber of commerce of greater Sorel, Mr. Henri Ollivier stressed the important economic advantages which could be derived from the deepening of the Richelieu river. Numerous steps were also taken in that connection by the late Dr. C. Robert Fiset, former mayor of Sorel, who worked intensively in that respect.
The St. John chamber of commerce submitted two briefs to the international boundary waters commission during the latter's sittings in the city of St. John in the riding now represented by the Minister without Portfolio.
Mr. Speaker, since the Associate Minister of National Defence and the Minister without Portfolio advocated the implementation of that project a few years ago, I wonder what they are doing now in this connection. That is why I am asking the minister to render them at least a service, to help with their reelection, if possible, while looking after the interests of the Canadian people.

Moreover, I ask the minister to tell us what serious objections the government would have to proceeding without delay, jointly with the United States, to the deepening of the Richelieu river?

subtopic: RICHELIEU WATERWAY
subsubtopic: STUDY BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks about the progress of the studies concerning the Richelieu deep waterway project. I must tell him that since the governments of Canada and the United States asked the international joint commission to make an inquiry as to whether the project was feasible and beneficial from an economic point of view, it held public hearings in the area concerned on both sides of the boundary. The commission also appointed a board of experts
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion which is now pursuing its work and technical investigation. The commission expects to receive from the investigation board a preliminary report on the feasibility of the project by June 1965. When it receives that report, the commission may take a decision as to the "form" of its own report to the two governments, and the date when it will be submitted.
We will consider seriously the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, who so efficiently supported the representations of various members on the government side.
